items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Executive summary paragraph for a pentest that found SQL injection on login page (Critical), missing security headers (Low), outdated Apache version (Medium). Example: 'During the assessment of your customer portal between 1-5 June, three categories of security issues were identified. The most significant is a critical SQL injection vulnerability in the user login form, which allows an unauthenticated attacker to bypass authentication and access any account, including administrative accounts. Successful exploitation would expose the full customer database and grant the attacker the same access as your trusted users. This issue requires immediate remediation. We also found that the web server is running an outdated version of Apache (2.4.41, released in 2019) with two publicly known security advisories — a software update is recommended within the next maintenance window. Finally, the portal does not set several HTTP security headers (Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security, X-Frame-Options); while these do not introduce direct vulnerabilities, they weaken the browser's defences against future client-side attacks and should be added as part of routine hardening. Full reproduction steps and remediation guidance for each issue follow in the technical findings.' Note what is and is not here: business impact in plain English (no CVSS numbers, no acronyms), priority ordering by risk to the company, no jargon. The CFO reads this paragraph and understands what to authorise.

mastery_questions: Executive summary paragraph for a pentest that found SQL injection on login page (Critical), missing security headers (Low), outdated Apache version (Medium). Example: 'During the assessment of your customer portal between 1-5 June, three categories of security issues were identified. The most significant is a critical SQL injection vulnerability in the user login form, which allows an unauthenticated attacker to bypass authentication and access any account, including administrative accounts. Successful exploitation would expose the full customer database and grant the attacker the same access as your trusted users. This issue requires immediate remediation. We also found that the web server is running an outdated version of Apache (2.4.41, released in 2019) with two publicly known security advisories — a software update is recommended within the next maintenance window. Finally, the portal does not set several HTTP security headers (Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security, X-Frame-Options); while these do not introduce direct vulnerabilities, they weaken the browser's defences against future client-side attacks and should be added as part of routine hardening. Full reproduction steps and remediation guidance for each issue follow in the technical findings.' Note what is and is not here: business impact in plain English (no CVSS numbers, no acronyms), priority ordering by risk to the company, no jargon. The CFO reads this paragraph and understands what to authorise.

Severity is a property of the vulnerability itself — the attacker capability and the impact if exploited, typically expressed via CVSS. Risk is the probability that the vulnerability will be exploited combined with the impact to YOUR business if it is. A Low severity bug with High risk: an information-disclosure issue (CVSS 3.5 — Low) reveals the existence of internal staging endpoints (`staging-api.company.com`). Severity is genuinely low — no immediate compromise. But: those staging endpoints have weak authentication, are connected to production data, and are being actively probed by a known threat actor that has been targeting your industry for months. Combined with credentials harvested from a separate phishing campaign two weeks ago, the disclosure provides the exact attack surface the threat actor needs to pivot into your production environment. The Low severity bug now sits at the centre of a High risk threat scenario. Risk = severity × exposure × threat intent × business impact. Severity is one of four factors. This is why mature security teams do not patch strictly by CVSS — they consider the active threat landscape, the asset's business value, and the attacker capability they actually face.

A developer reads your XSS remediation and says 'just sanitise the input'. This is wrong — at least incomplete and at worst dangerous — for two reasons. (1) 'Sanitisation' (stripping or escaping characters at input time) is fragile because the right escaping depends on the OUTPUT context, not the input. The same string `<script>` needs different handling if it ends up in HTML body (escape as `<script>`), HTML attribute (escape quotes, ampersand, less-than), JavaScript string literal (escape backslash, quote, less-than, slash), CSS context (escape carefully or reject entirely), or URL parameter (URL-encode). Input sanitisation that escapes for HTML breaks the data when it later appears in JSON. Output encoding handles each context correctly. (2) Input sanitisation assumes you control every code path that uses the data. As soon as a new feature uses the same database field in a new context (the user's bio displayed in an HTML page, then in a JSON API, then in an email), the old sanitisation is insufficient. The correct remediation: encode at output time using context-aware encoders (your framework provides them: React escapes by default, Django templates auto-escape, Rails `<%= %>` auto-escapes). Treat all stored data as potentially-hostile and encode whenever it enters a sensitive context. This pattern (output encoding) is what scales.

Explaining CVSS scoring to a non-technical executive without using the acronym: 'When we find a security issue, we score it on a scale from 0 to 10 based on three things: how easily an attacker could exploit it, how much access they would gain if they did, and how much damage they could cause. A score of 9 or 10 means a remote attacker could take complete control with minimal effort — these need to be fixed within 24-48 hours. A score of 7 or 8 means the attacker needs some preconditions (user has to click a link, attacker needs a low-privilege account first) but the impact is still severe — fix within a week. A score of 4-6 means either the impact is contained (data leak rather than takeover) or the exploit is non-trivial (needs physical access, complex attack chain) — fix within a month. Below 4 is good to fix but not urgent. The score is a global standard — every security professional understands it — but the right priority for YOUR business depends on more than the number. A 9 on a system that handles customer payments is more urgent than a 9 on an internal HR tool used by three people.' What did this avoid? The acronym CVSS, the term 'vector string', the words 'integrity' and 'confidentiality' as security terms. Plain English plus business context.

Executive summary content vs technical findings content. The executive summary contains: business impact (what could happen to the company), risk ratings in plain English (Critical / High / Medium / Low), a short prioritised list of categories of issues found, recommended business actions (engage incident response, allocate engineering capacity, brief leadership), the timebox and scope of the assessment. It does NOT contain: CVE numbers, CVSS vectors, payload strings, HTTP requests, code snippets, tool names like sqlmap or Burp, line numbers in source files, parameter names. The technical findings contain: per-finding ID, title, severity rating with CVSS vector, affected component and version, full reproduction steps with HTTP requests and responses, evidence (screenshots, log excerpts), impact analysis specific to this finding, remediation with code-level guidance (which library, which configuration, which patch). It does NOT contain: business narrative, executive opinion, generic 'security is important' framing, full CVSS theory explanations (link to the CVSS calculator instead). The bright line: an executive reads the summary in 5 minutes and knows what to authorise. A developer reads ONE finding in 15 minutes and knows exactly what to change. Mixing the two creates a report that is too long for the executive and too vague for the developer — both audiences ignore it.
weeks.ai_assist:
**Prompts that work:**
- "Review this vulnerability finding and improve the remediation section: [paste your finding]"
- "Help me write an executive summary for a pentest with these findings: [list findings with severity]"
- "What is the correct remediation for stored XSS in a React application? Be specific about which library to use and how."
- "How do I explain the business impact of an IDOR vulnerability to a non-technical CEO in 2 sentences?"
weeks.stakeholder_moment: Bug bounty report audience is a triager who has 30 seconds + a junior developer who has 30 minutes to fix. The triager wants: severity + quick repro. The dev wants: clear steps + suggested fix. Write for both.
weeks.pre_flight:
**Read these real pentest reports (public, redacted):**
- Cure53 public reports: https://cure53.de/#publications
- NCC Group public advisories: https://research.nccgroup.com/

**Report structure to memorise:**
```
1. Title Page
2. Table of Contents
3. Executive Summary (1 page, non-technical)
   - Scope and Objectives
   - Overall Risk Rating
   - Key Findings Summary (3-5 bullets)
   - Strategic Recommendations
4. Technical Findings
   - Finding 1: Title, Severity, CVSS, Description, Steps, Impact, Remediation, Evidence
   - Finding 2: ...
5. Appendix
   - Methodology
   - Tools Used
   - Scope Details
```

**Tools for report writing:**
- Notion or Obsidian: note-taking during testing
- PlexTrac, Dradis, or Sysreptor: professional report platforms
- For now: Markdown + PDF export is fine
common_mistakes: Writing one report for both audiences — executives do not read CVSS vector strings; developers do not need business risk narratives. Split them clearly.
Copying CVE descriptions as your finding description — you must describe the vulnerability as it exists in the specific application you tested, not generically.
Not including evidence — 'we found SQL injection' without a screenshot or HTTP request is not a valid report finding.
Recommending 'upgrade to the latest version' without checking what the latest version is and if it is stable for production.
Delivering findings verbally without a written report — verbal findings cannot be tracked, assigned, or closed. Always deliver in writing.
weeks.debug_help:
**Not sure how to write the remediation?**
Start with: 'The remediation is to [specific action] using [specific library/config]. Here is an example: [code snippet].'
Never write: 'Fix the SQL injection.' That is not remediation.

**Struggling with risk rating?**
Use this framework:
- Critical: directly exploitable, significant data loss or system compromise, no authentication required
- High: exploitable but requires some conditions, significant impact
- Medium: exploitable with significant conditions, moderate impact, or low-impact with easy exploit
- Low: theoretical or requires many conditions to exploit, minimal impact
- Info: no direct security risk, but relevant context

**Report template starting point:**
Copy a Cure53 report structure and use it as your template.

weeks.title: Defence Basics — Logging, SIEM, Detection
weeks.context:
Security is not only about attack. The other half of the field is defence — detecting, alerting, and responding to attacks. This week you switch to the defender's perspective and learn the core tools: logging, SIEM (Security Information and Event Management), and detection engineering.

Logs are the foundation of security operations. Every login attempt, every HTTP request, every system call generates a log. A SIEM collects logs from across an environment, normalises them, and applies detection rules to find suspicious patterns. Without logs, you cannot detect attacks.

You learn Elastic SIEM (free, open-source) or Splunk (free tier) this week. You ingest logs, write detection queries, and build a basic alert. Even as an offensive security specialist, understanding how defenders detect you makes you a better attacker.
topics: What to log — auth events, sensitive operations, anomalies
Log centralisation — syslog, Filebeat/Vector, Loki/Elasticsearch
SIEM concepts — Security Information and Event Management
Elastic Stack — Elasticsearch + Kibana + Beats
Splunk — the enterprise SIEM; powerful + expensive
Wazuh — open-source SIEM + HIDS
Detection engineering — Sigma rules as detection-as-code
Alert fatigue — the real failure mode of every SOC

Trigger some attacker-like behaviour (failed SSH logins, scan); verify Wazuh detects
Write 5 Sigma detection rules for common attack patterns
Set up alert routing to a chat channel (Slack, Discord)

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Picture your lab right now: the firewall keeps one log, each VM keeps its own, the web app keeps another — all in different formats, all on different machines. A SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) is the tool that ingests all of those, normalises them into one common shape so a Windows login and a Linux login become comparable, and then hunts the combined stream for patterns no single box could see alone. The reason this matters is correlation — a failed login here plus a success there plus a file copied somewhere else looks innocent on each machine but screams 'breach' when you line all three up on one timeline. Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel and Elastic are three you will meet in industry, but the tool is the easy part. Tell me in your own words: what can a SIEM detect that you could never spot by reading each machine's logs separately?

mastery_questions: Picture your lab right now: the firewall keeps one log, each VM keeps its own, the web app keeps another — all in different formats, all on different machines. A SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) is the tool that ingests all of those, normalises them into one common shape so a Windows login and a Linux login become comparable, and then hunts the combined stream for patterns no single box could see alone. The reason this matters is correlation — a failed login here plus a success there plus a file copied somewhere else looks innocent on each machine but screams 'breach' when you line all three up on one timeline. Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel and Elastic are three you will meet in industry, but the tool is the easy part. Tell me in your own words: what can a SIEM detect that you could never spot by reading each machine's logs separately?

A log and an alert are not the same thing, and confusing them is the first mistake every junior makes. A log is a passive record — 'user X logged in at 04:02' — written whether or not anyone ever reads it; your servers generate millions a day and almost all are noise. An alert is an active claim that something is worth a human's attention right now — it is a rule you wrote that fired because the log stream matched a suspicious pattern. A good alert rule is specific enough that when it fires you genuinely care, and quiet enough that it does not cry wolf — it has a clear hypothesis ('this pattern means an attacker is doing X') and a defined action for whoever receives it. Take one rule from your home SOC and answer honestly: when this fires at 3am, will the on-call engineer know exactly what happened and what to do — or will they snooze it?

A false positive is an alert that fires when nothing bad actually happened — the rule matched, but the activity was legitimate. It sounds harmless until you do the arithmetic. Say your SOC processes 1,000,000 events a day and your detection rule has a 'mere' 10% false-positive rate against the slice of events that look vaguely suspicious — that is still thousands of bogus alerts landing in an analyst's queue every single day. The human cannot triage thousands, so they start ignoring the channel, and the one real attack scrolls past unread: this is alert fatigue, and it is how breaches happen in companies that 'had detection in place'. Look at your noisiest rule and tell me — at your event volume, how many false alerts does it generate per day, and at what number does a real human stop looking?

A Sigma rule is detection-as-code — a YAML description of a suspicious pattern written in a vendor-neutral format, so the same rule can be translated into a Splunk search, an Elastic query, or a Wazuh decoder without rewriting it for each. The power is portability: you describe the behaviour once, share it with the world, and everyone's SIEM can use it. Let's build one for brute-force: you want it to fire when the same source IP produces, say, 10 or more failed-login events inside 5 minutes — so your rule needs a detection block matching the failed-auth event, a timeframe, and a condition that counts selection grouped by src_ip above the threshold. Sketch that rule for me, and then tell me the one thing about it that would generate false positives in the real world (hint: think about what a misconfigured backup script or a corporate NAT gateway looks like to your counter).

Detecting a successful SQL injection is not about one log — it is about correlating three. Your web server log shows the request that came in (a URL or POST body carrying a suspicious OR 1=1 or a UNION SELECT); your database log shows the query that actually executed and whether it returned an abnormal number of rows; and your application or response log shows whether the attacker got data back (a sudden 200 with a giant response body where a 401 was expected). No single one of these proves a breach — a weird URL might be blocked, a big query might be a report — but the three together tell the story of input then execution then exfiltration. Walk me through which log sources you would need wired into your SOC to reconstruct that chain, and which single source most teams forget to collect.

**Basic Elastic query (KQL):**
```
# Find all failed SSH logins
event.action: "authentication_failure" and service.type: "ssh"

# Find HTTP 4xx errors
```

common_mistakes: Logging everything without a retention policy — logs cost money to store. Define what you log, for how long, and at what level.
Writing detection rules without tuning them — a rule that fires 1,000 times a day is ignored. Tune rules to have high signal-to-noise ratio.
Not logging failed authentication attempts — successful logins are not the threat. Failed logins (especially in bursts) are the signal.
Ignoring log integrity — logs must be shipped to a central system immediately. An attacker who compromises a host can delete local logs.
Alert fatigue is a real security risk — too many alerts means analysts stop reading them. Prioritise ruthlessly.

weeks.title: Incident Response Basics — When Something Real Happens
weeks.context:
Incidents happen. The question is not whether you will face a security incident but whether you have a plan when you do. Incident Response (IR) is the structured process of detecting, containing, eradicating, and recovering from a security breach.

The IR lifecycle: Preparation → Detection → Analysis → Containment → Eradication → Recovery → Post-Incident Review. Most organisations are terrible at Preparation and Post-Incident Review, which means they keep having the same incidents.

This week you learn the IR process, how to triage an incident (what is compromised, how far has it spread, what data is at risk), and how to write a post-incident report. You also learn basic forensics: how to preserve evidence, read system logs, and establish a timeline.
topics: The SANS IR lifecycle — 6 phases, what each means
First responder actions — preserve evidence, isolate, document
Memory forensics with Volatility
Disk imaging — dd, FTK Imager, chain of custody
Log timeline analysis — correlating events across systems
Containment strategies — short-term vs long-term
Communication during an incident — who needs to know, when
Post-incident — RCAs, learnings, hardening
tasks: Read the SANS IR Handler's Handbook
Use Volatility to analyse a memory dump from a HackTheBox forensics challenge
Use dd to image a small disk; verify the hash
Practice a tabletop incident: 'Suspicious authentication from foreign IP' — walk through your IR playbook
Write an IR runbook for one realistic scenario

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Incident response has a lifecycle, and the discipline is in knowing which phase you are in so you do not, for example, start wiping machines (eradication) before you have figured out how far the attacker spread (analysis). The six phases are Preparation, Detection, Analysis, Containment, Eradication, Recovery, and the Post-Incident Review — and most organisations are genuinely good at the middle and genuinely terrible at the first and last, which is exactly why they keep suffering the same breach twice. Let's thread one story through it: a developer's laptop gets phished. Preparation is the EDR and the runbook you wrote before it happened; Detection is the alert that fired; Analysis is you scoping what the malware touched; Containment is isolating that laptop; Eradication is removing the implant; Recovery is safely bringing the user back online; and the Review is the meeting where you ask why the phish got through. Take that same phished-laptop scenario and tell me: which phase, done badly, turns a one-laptop incident into a company-wide one?

mastery_questions: Incident response has a lifecycle, and the discipline is in knowing which phase you are in so you do not, for example, start wiping machines (eradication) before you have figured out how far the attacker spread (analysis). The six phases are Preparation, Detection, Analysis, Containment, Eradication, Recovery, and the Post-Incident Review — and most organisations are genuinely good at the middle and genuinely terrible at the first and last, which is exactly why they keep suffering the same breach twice. Let's thread one story through it: a developer's laptop gets phished. Preparation is the EDR and the runbook you wrote before it happened; Detection is the alert that fired; Analysis is you scoping what the malware touched; Containment is isolating that laptop; Eradication is removing the implant; Recovery is safely bringing the user back online; and the Review is the meeting where you ask why the phish got through. Take that same phished-laptop scenario and tell me: which phase, done badly, turns a one-laptop incident into a company-wide one?

You are on call. An alert fires: a server is sending unusual outbound traffic to a foreign IP at 3am. Before you touch anything, understand the instinct you must fight — the urge to immediately pull the plug, because a panicked reaction can destroy the very evidence you will need and tip off the attacker. So your first moves are about observe-then-act: confirm the alert is real (is this actually anomalous, or a backup job you forgot about?), capture volatile evidence (current connections, running processes, memory) before it vanishes, identify what the box is and what it can reach, decide whether to contain by isolating rather than powering off, and start a timeline document from the very first minute. Give me your ordered first five steps for this exact alert, and justify why 'reboot the server' is nowhere on your list.

Forensic preservation is the practice of capturing evidence in a way that you can later prove was not altered — because the moment you start poking at a live system, you change it, and a changed system is a contaminated crime scene. The classic rule is that you image a drive — make a bit-for-bit copy — before you analyse it, and you work only on the copy, leaving the original untouched and hashed so you can prove it is identical. Why bother, when you just want to find the malware? Because if this incident ever becomes a legal matter, an insurance claim, or a dispute about what the attacker accessed, evidence you mutated while 'just looking' is worthless — and you often do not know an incident is legally significant until weeks later. Explain to me what specifically changes on a running system the moment you log in and start browsing folders, and why that is a problem for the timeline you are trying to build.

Chain of custody is the documented, unbroken record of who handled a piece of evidence, when, and what they did with it — from the moment it was collected to the moment it is presented. Think of it as the evidence's own logbook: imaged the drive at 04:12, hashed it (SHA-256: abc...), stored it in a locked location, transferred to analyst Y at 09:00 who verified the hash matched. It matters because evidence with a gap in its custody chain can be challenged — if there is an hour where nobody can prove where the drive was or that it was not tampered with, an opposing lawyer (or a sceptical auditor) can argue it was planted or altered, and your whole investigation collapses. In your IR playbook, who is responsible for starting the custody log, and at what exact moment does the clock start?

Scoping a compromise means answering the question every executive asks first: 'how bad is it — what did they touch?'. You determine it by pivoting outward from the known-bad: you have one compromised host, so you ask what credentials lived on it, what it could reach on the network, what it authenticated to, and whether those same indicators (a malicious IP, a file hash, an attacker tool) appear anywhere else. Your log sources are the map — authentication logs to trace credential reuse, network and firewall logs to trace lateral movement, EDR telemetry to trace process lineage, and your SIEM to search all of them at once for the attacker's fingerprints. The hardest part is knowing when you have found the edge of the blast radius versus when you just have not looked far enough. Given one compromised laptop in your lab, walk me through how you would expand outward to decide whether the attacker reached your domain controller.

**IR playbook template:**
```markdown
# Incident Response Playbook — [Incident Type]

## Detection
- Alert source:
- Initial indicator:
- Time detected:

## Triage Questions
1. What systems are affected?
2. Is the attacker still active?
3. What data may be compromised?
4. What is the business impact?

## Containment Steps
1. Isolate affected systems
2. Preserve logs before they rotate
3. Change compromised credentials

## Eradication
- Remove malware/backdoors
- Patch exploited vulnerability
- Verify no persistence mechanisms remain

## Recovery
- Restore from known-good backup
- Monitor for re-compromise
- Verify normal operation

## Post-Incident Review
- Timeline of events
- Root cause
- What we did well / what we missed
- Action items with owners and deadlines
```
common_mistakes: Eradicating before containing — if you clean a machine before isolating it from the network, you lose the evidence AND the attacker may still have access.
Not preserving logs before containment — rotating logs and rebooting systems destroys forensic evidence. Preserve first, then act.
Treating every alert as an incident — not every alert is an incident. Triage determines if it is a true positive requiring IR vs a false positive.
Skipping the post-incident review — this is the most valuable part. Without it, the same incident happens again.
Not communicating during the incident — stakeholders need regular updates even if you have nothing new to report. 'We are investigating, update in 1 hour' is valid.
weeks.debug_help:
**Building a timeline from logs:**
```bash
# Find all events in a time range in auth.log
grep "Mar 15 02:" /var/log/auth.log
# Find all commands run by a user (bash history)
cat /home/username/.bash_history
# Find recently modified files (last 24 hours)
find / -mtime -1 -type f 2>/dev/null | head -50
# Find files with SUID bit (common persistence technique)
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null
```

**Volatility for memory forensics:**
```bash
# Install Volatility 3
pip install volatility3
# List processes from a memory image
vol -f memory.dmp windows.pslist
# Find network connections
vol -f memory.dmp windows.netstat
```

weeks.title: Endpoint Security — EDR, Hardening, MDM
weeks.context:
Endpoints — laptops, servers, mobile devices — are where most attacks land. Phishing delivers malware to a laptop. A compromised server is an endpoint. Endpoint security is the practice of hardening these devices and monitoring them for malicious activity.

EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) is the modern evolution of antivirus. Instead of signature matching, EDR monitors system behaviour: process creation, network connections, file writes, registry changes. When a process does something suspicious (like spawning PowerShell from Word), the EDR flags it.

This week you learn how defenders harden endpoints (CIS Benchmarks, Group Policy on Windows, sysctl on Linux) and how attackers bypass these controls. Understanding bypass techniques as a defender helps you build better detections.
topics: OS hardening baselines — CIS Benchmarks for Linux + Windows + macOS
EDR fundamentals — what it sees that AV doesn't
Open-source EDR — Wazuh, Velociraptor, Falcon (free agents)
Application allowlisting — when to use, the operational tax
Disk encryption — FileVault, BitLocker, LUKS
MDM — Jamf (Mac), Intune (Windows), Kandji
BYOD vs corporate-issued — the policy debate
Mobile device security — iOS vs Android security models
tasks: Apply a CIS Benchmark Level 1 to one of your Ubuntu VMs; document deviations
Install Velociraptor on a test endpoint; run a hunt for a suspicious file
Configure FileVault (Mac) or BitLocker (Windows); verify encryption is active
Set up an MDM trial (Jamf Now, Kandji, or InTune); enroll a test device
Compare what Falcon, SentinelOne, MS Defender for Endpoint report on the same suspicious behaviour

Install an EDR (Falcon free tier or Wazuh agent). Document the baseline in HARDENING.md. This is what every developer should have on day 1.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Traditional antivirus and EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) answer two different questions. Antivirus asks 'have I seen this exact bad file before?' — it matches files against a database of known-malware signatures, which means a brand-new or slightly-modified malware sails straight past it. EDR asks a smarter question: 'is this program behaving like an attacker?' — it watches behaviour, like a Word document spawning PowerShell, or a process reaching into another process's memory, or a binary suddenly making network connections it never made before. The shift matters because modern attackers do not drop a known virus; they abuse legitimate tools and live off the land, which is invisible to signatures but glaring to behavioural monitoring. Give me one concrete attack that AV would completely miss but EDR would catch, and explain what behaviour gives it away.

mastery_questions: Traditional antivirus and EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) answer two different questions. Antivirus asks 'have I seen this exact bad file before?' — it matches files against a database of known-malware signatures, which means a brand-new or slightly-modified malware sails straight past it. EDR asks a smarter question: 'is this program behaving like an attacker?' — it watches behaviour, like a Word document spawning PowerShell, or a process reaching into another process's memory, or a binary suddenly making network connections it never made before. The shift matters because modern attackers do not drop a known virus; they abuse legitimate tools and live off the land, which is invisible to signatures but glaring to behavioural monitoring. Give me one concrete attack that AV would completely miss but EDR would catch, and explain what behaviour gives it away.

Windows writes thousands of event types, but a handful are the ones a defender lives by — and knowing why each matters is more useful than memorising the numbers. Think about what an attacker actually does: they log in (4624 successful logon, 4625 failed logon — a flood of 4625s then one 4624 is brute-force succeeding), they escalate or create accounts (4720 account created, 4672 special privileges assigned), and they run things (4688 process creation, especially with command-line logging on). The skill is not reciting IDs — it is mapping an attacker action to the event that betrays it. Pick five of these, tell me what each logs, and for one of them describe the exact attacker behaviour that would make it light up in your SOC.

A CIS Benchmark is a community-built, consensus checklist of secure-configuration settings for a specific system — 'on Ubuntu, set this, disable that' — published by the Center for Internet Security and used as the baseline that auditors and hardening guides point to. The value is that you do not have to invent 'what does secure look like' from scratch; experts already argued it out and wrote it down. But a checklist you apply blindly is just cargo-culting — the skill is understanding why each control reduces risk. Pick one real control from the CIS Ubuntu benchmark (say, disabling SSH root login, or setting a password-aging policy) and explain to me, in attacker terms, exactly what that one setting takes away from someone trying to break in.

LOLBAS — Living Off The Land Binaries And Scripts — is the attacker technique of using the legitimate tools already installed on a system to do their dirty work, instead of bringing their own malware that an EDR would flag. Why write a custom downloader when certutil.exe or bitsadmin can fetch a file, powershell can run anything in memory, and rundll32 can execute code — all signed by Microsoft, all expected to be there, all trusted by default. This is the heart of why behavioural detection beats signature detection: the binary is innocent, so you have to catch the unusual way it is being used. Name three legitimate Windows tools attackers abuse this way, and for one of them tell me what the normal use looks like versus the malicious use — because that gap is exactly what your detection has to spot.

Process injection is when an attacker runs their malicious code inside the memory space of a legitimate, trusted process — so that to the casual observer, it is explorer.exe or a browser doing the bad thing, not some suspicious new binary. They do it to hide and to inherit the trust and permissions of the host process. The good news for a defender is that injection is not free — it requires specific, unusual API calls (opening a handle to another process, allocating executable memory inside it, writing code there, and starting a thread to run it), and an EDR sitting at the kernel level can see exactly that sequence. So the detectable artefact is not the code itself — it is the act of one process reaching into another. Describe the chain of operations an injection leaves behind, and tell me why a legitimate program almost never does that sequence.

**Linux hardening quick audit:**
```bash
# Check for world-writable files
find / -xdev -type f -perm -0002 2>/dev/null

# Check SUID binaries
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null

# Check listening services
ss -tlnp

# Check cron jobs (potential persistence)
crontab -l
ls /etc/cron.*

# Check users with shell access
grep -v '/sbin/nologin|/bin/false' /etc/passwd
```

common_mistakes: Treating hardening as a one-time task — configurations drift. Run hardening checks continuously or on every deploy.
Blocking legitimate admin tools to reduce attack surface — this creates operational friction. Use allowlisting with context, not blanket blocking.
Ignoring endpoint telemetry — an EDR that nobody monitors is worthless. Alerts need to route to a SOC or a human who can act.
Not testing your detections — write a detection rule, then simulate the attack to confirm the rule fires. Untested detections give false confidence.
Underestimating LOLBAS — attackers who use PowerShell, certutil, and mshta are harder to detect than those who drop custom malware.

```bash
# Verify manager connection

```

```bash

# View audit log
```

weeks.title: Threat Intelligence and Hunting
weeks.context:
Threat intelligence is information about adversaries — who they are, what they want, what tools they use, and how they operate. Threat hunting is proactively searching your environment for signs of compromise that automated tools have not detected.

Most security teams are reactive: they respond to alerts. Threat hunters are proactive: they form a hypothesis ('I think an attacker might be using WMI for persistence') and go hunting for evidence of that technique across all their endpoint telemetry.

This week you learn the threat intelligence lifecycle, how to consume and apply threat feeds (IOCs, TTPs), and how to run a basic threat hunt using MITRE ATT&CK as your framework. You also learn about threat actor groups — understanding your likely adversaries changes how you prioritise defences.
topics: Threat intelligence — strategic, operational, tactical levels
MITRE ATT&CK — using it for hunt hypotheses
IOCs (Indicators of Compromise) — hashes, IPs, domains, URLs
TTPs (Tactics, Techniques, Procedures) — why these beat IOCs
Threat-intel feeds — MISP, ThreatFox, AlienVault OTX
Threat hunting methodology — hypothesis-driven
Sigma + YARA — detection-as-code at different layers
OSINT for security teams — daily threat news, attribution

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Threat intelligence comes in three altitudes, and the mistake is handing the wrong altitude to the wrong person. Strategic intel is the boardroom view — 'ransomware groups are increasingly targeting our industry' — consumed by executives to decide where to spend money. Operational intel is the campaign view — 'this specific group is active and uses these tactics against companies like ours' — consumed by security leadership to prioritise defences. Tactical intel is the trench view — 'here is the exact IP, hash, and command the attacker uses' — consumed by analysts and your SIEM to build detections right now. The same breach generates all three; the skill is translating up and down the ladder. Give me one real threat and write the strategic, operational, and tactical version of it — and tell me who reads each.

mastery_questions: Threat intelligence comes in three altitudes, and the mistake is handing the wrong altitude to the wrong person. Strategic intel is the boardroom view — 'ransomware groups are increasingly targeting our industry' — consumed by executives to decide where to spend money. Operational intel is the campaign view — 'this specific group is active and uses these tactics against companies like ours' — consumed by security leadership to prioritise defences. Tactical intel is the trench view — 'here is the exact IP, hash, and command the attacker uses' — consumed by analysts and your SIEM to build detections right now. The same breach generates all three; the skill is translating up and down the ladder. Give me one real threat and write the strategic, operational, and tactical version of it — and tell me who reads each.

An IOC (Indicator of Compromise) is a specific artefact — a file hash, an IP address, a domain — while a TTP (Tactic, Technique, Procedure) describes the attacker's behaviour — 'they use spear-phishing to deliver a macro that establishes persistence via a scheduled task'. The Pyramid of Pain explains why TTPs are worth more: an attacker can change a file hash in seconds and a domain in minutes — those IOCs have a shelf life measured in hours. But changing how they operate — their actual techniques — is expensive and painful, so a detection built on behaviour keeps catching them long after the indicators have rotated. This is why mature teams hunt for techniques, not just block bad IPs. Take a known attacker, give me one IOC and one TTP for them, and tell me which one you would rather have your detection built on six months from now, and why.

MITRE ATT&CK is a giant, structured catalogue of how real attackers actually behave, organised so you can speak a common language with the rest of the industry. The hierarchy matters: a Tactic is the attacker's goal — the 'why', like Persistence or Lateral Movement; a Technique is the how — the general method, like 'Scheduled Task' for achieving persistence; and a Sub-technique is a specific variant of that method. Think of it as why then how then exactly-how. The framework's power is that it turns 'we got hacked' into 'the adversary used T1053.005 for persistence', which everyone — your team, your vendors, threat reports — instantly understands. Pick a tactic, name a technique under it and a sub-technique under that, and explain how you would use that single entry to drive a hunt in your own logs.

Threat hunting is the opposite of waiting for an alert — you start with a hypothesis ('I believe an attacker might be doing X in my environment right now') and go looking for evidence, whether or not any tool flagged it. The hypothesis has to be specific and testable, grounded in a real technique, and tied to data you actually collect — a vague 'maybe someone is in here' is not a hunt. For lateral movement, a strong hypothesis might be: 'if an attacker is moving between machines using stolen credentials, I should see the same account authenticating to multiple hosts it never normally touches, in a short window'. Now you know exactly which logs to query and what 'found it' looks like. Write me a hunting hypothesis for detecting lateral movement in your lab, and tell me precisely which log and which pattern would confirm or kill it.

Attribution is the attempt to answer 'who did this?' — tying an attack to a specific group or nation — and it is genuinely hard because everything an attacker leaves behind can be faked. They route through other victims' machines, reuse tools that other groups also use, plant false flags (foreign-language comments, foreign timezones) to mislead you, and the only people with high-confidence attribution usually have intelligence sources you do not. Here is the contrarian point worth wrestling with: for most defenders, attribution barely matters — knowing that it was 'APT-Whoever' does not change the fact that you need to detect the technique and kick them out. Tell me when attribution genuinely does matter to a decision-maker, and when chasing it is just an expensive distraction from defending.

common_mistakes: Chasing IOC hashes without context — a malware hash is the least useful IOC. Attackers recompile malware daily. TTPs persist for years.
Treating all threat intelligence as equally relevant — a threat feed full of Chinese APT IOCs is not useful if you are a small retail company. Contextualise to your threat model.
Hunting without a hypothesis — randomly looking through logs is not threat hunting. Start with a specific technique and look for its artefacts.
Not documenting hunts — record your hypothesis, what you searched, what you found, and your conclusion. This builds institutional knowledge.
Confusing threat intelligence with vulnerability intelligence — CVEs are not threat intelligence. Threat intel is about adversary behaviour.

weeks.title: Cloud Security — AWS, Azure, GCP
weeks.context:
Cloud infrastructure is now the default for most companies. Cloud security is fundamentally different from on-premise security: the attack surface is configuration, not physical access. Most cloud breaches happen because of misconfigured S3 buckets, overly permissive IAM roles, or exposed metadata endpoints — not because an attacker broke into a data centre.

This week you learn the cloud security fundamentals: shared responsibility model, IAM policies, network security groups, and the most common cloud misconfigurations. You will audit an AWS environment for security issues using tools like ScoutSuite, Prowler, and AWS Config.

The mindset shift: in cloud, your infrastructure is code (Terraform, CloudFormation). Security misconfigurations in that code are vulnerabilities, just like SQL injection in application code.
topics: Shared Responsibility Model — what AWS secures, what you secure
IAM attack paths — over-permissive policies, instance profile abuse, role chaining
Public S3 buckets — how they happen, how to detect
Secrets in code — git, S3, EBS snapshots, AMIs
Cloud-native scanners — Prowler, ScoutSuite, Steampipe
AWS-specific attacks — Pacu, CloudGoat
GCP attack paths — pwning Google Cloud
Defence — CloudTrail, GuardDuty, AWS Config, IAM Access Analyzer
tasks: Set up CloudGoat (a vulnerable AWS environment); complete 2 scenarios
Run Pacu against your CloudGoat instance; understand the attack modules
Run Prowler against your real AWS account; fix the top 5 HIGH findings
Enable GuardDuty + CloudTrail; trigger a finding deliberately; verify alert
Configure IAM Access Analyzer; resolve every finding

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: The Shared Responsibility Model is the single most misunderstood line in cloud security, and getting it wrong is how companies end up breached while believing 'AWS handles security'. The split is roughly: AWS secures the cloud itself — the physical data centres, the hardware, the hypervisor, the managed-service infrastructure — while you secure what you put in the cloud — your data, your IAM permissions, your network rules, your patching, your S3 bucket settings. The line moves depending on the service: with raw EC2 you patch the OS; with a managed database AWS patches it but you still control who can access it. The dangerous gap is assuming the provider covers something they explicitly do not — like access control on your own data. Pick one AWS service and draw the exact line for me: name one thing AWS secures and one thing that, if you get it wrong, is entirely your breach.

mastery_questions: The Shared Responsibility Model is the single most misunderstood line in cloud security, and getting it wrong is how companies end up breached while believing 'AWS handles security'. The split is roughly: AWS secures the cloud itself — the physical data centres, the hardware, the hypervisor, the managed-service infrastructure — while you secure what you put in the cloud — your data, your IAM permissions, your network rules, your patching, your S3 bucket settings. The line moves depending on the service: with raw EC2 you patch the OS; with a managed database AWS patches it but you still control who can access it. The dangerous gap is assuming the provider covers something they explicitly do not — like access control on your own data. Pick one AWS service and draw the exact line for me: name one thing AWS secures and one thing that, if you get it wrong, is entirely your breach.

An IAM user is a permanent identity with long-lived credentials — like a named employee with their own keys — while an IAM role is a set of permissions that can be temporarily assumed by whoever needs them, handing out short-lived credentials that expire. The security reason to prefer roles is that long-lived keys are the thing that leaks: they get committed to GitHub, baked into AMIs, left in config files, and once leaked they work forever until someone notices. A role assumed by an EC2 instance (via an instance profile) means the instance gets rotating temporary credentials and there is no static secret to steal. So the rule of thumb: humans and services should assume roles, not carry permanent keys. Give me a concrete situation where someone reaches for an IAM user, and explain how a role solves the same need more safely.

A publicly readable S3 bucket is the most common cloud breach in history — not because of clever hacking, but because someone clicked 'make public' or misconfigured a policy, and suddenly customer data, backups, or secrets are downloadable by anyone who finds the URL. The risk is total: there is no login to brute-force, no exploit to write — the data is just there, often discovered by automated scanners that crawl S3 namespaces all day. To audit an account you do not eyeball buckets one by one; you use the account-level Block Public Access settings, IAM Access Analyzer, or a tool like Prowler to enumerate every bucket and flag any with public ACLs or policies. Tell me how you would audit all buckets in an account at once, and what the safest default setting is that makes a single misconfigured bucket impossible.

The IMDS (Instance Metadata Service) is a special address — 169.254.169.254 — that any EC2 instance can query to learn about itself, including, critically, the temporary credentials of the IAM role attached to it. That is convenient for the instance, but it is a goldmine for an attacker: if they find an SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery) vulnerability in your web app, they can trick your server into fetching that metadata URL and handing back its cloud credentials — which is exactly how the 2019 Capital One breach happened. The fix is IMDSv2, which requires a session token via a PUT request first, defeating the simple SSRF-fetch trick. Explain to me the attack chain from 'web app with SSRF' to 'attacker has your IAM credentials', and where IMDSv2 breaks that chain.

IAM privilege escalation is when an attacker who has landed with limited permissions uses those very permissions to grant themselves more — turning a foothold into admin without exploiting any software bug, just abusing the permission system's own logic. The classic example: say you have iam:PassRole and lambda:CreateFunction. Individually they look harmless, but together you can create a Lambda function, pass it a high-privilege role you are allowed to pass, and have that function run code as that powerful role — instant escalation. This is why least-privilege is not about big obvious permissions but about dangerous combinations. Walk me through that PassRole plus CreateFunction chain step by step, and tell me what you would check in a policy to spot escalation paths like it.

**CloudGoat — deliberately vulnerable AWS environment:**
```bash
# Rhino Security Labs' CloudGoat for practise
git clone https://github.com/RhinoSecurityLabs/cloudgoat
cd cloudgoat && pip install -r requirements.txt
./cloudgoat.py create iam_privesc_by_rollback
```

**Key AWS security concepts:**

- CloudTrail: API call audit logs

common_mistakes: Using the root account for daily operations — root has unlimited permissions and cannot be restricted. Create IAM users with least privilege immediately.
Storing credentials in application code or environment variables without using IAM roles — any code execution vulnerability exposes those credentials.
Leaving security groups open to 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22 or 3389 — SSH and RDP should never be open to the internet. Use VPN, bastion host, or SSM Session Manager.
Not enabling CloudTrail — without CloudTrail, you have no audit log of API calls. This is the first thing to turn on in any AWS account.
Assuming 'private' S3 means secure — check bucket policies, ACLs, and public access blocks. Multiple layers can each introduce exposure.

weeks.title: Container and Kubernetes Security
weeks.context:
Container security is now essential because most production workloads run in containers. A container is not a VM — it shares the host kernel. A container escape vulnerability means an attacker who compromises a container can potentially escape to the host and access all other containers.

Kubernetes adds another layer: the API server is the control plane for the entire cluster. A misconfigured RBAC policy or an exposed dashboard can give an attacker cluster-admin access. The 2019 Tesla cryptojacking breach happened because their Kubernetes dashboard had no authentication.

This week you learn container image security (scanning, base image choice), Kubernetes RBAC, Pod Security Standards, network policies, and how to use tools like Trivy, kubeaudit, and kube-bench to audit a cluster.
topics: Container escape vulnerabilities — runc CVEs, privileged containers
Capabilities — what each does, why you should drop most
AppArmor / SELinux profiles
Kubernetes RBAC — common mistakes, how attackers escalate
Pod Security Standards (replaced PSPs)
Network policies — default-deny, explicit allows
Image security — scanning, signing, admission control
Runtime security — Falco, Tetragon for kernel-level detection

Run a privileged container; demonstrate container escape via /proc
Install Falco on your local K8s; trigger detections by running suspicious commands
Apply restrictive Pod Security Standards to your namespace

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: A container escape is the nightmare scenario of containerisation: an attacker who has compromised the inside of a container breaks out to the host itself — and because every container on that host shares the same kernel, escaping to the host can mean owning every other container too. Remember the core fact that makes this possible: a container is not a VM; it is an isolated process sharing the host's kernel, so a kernel vulnerability or a too-generous configuration is a door out. Two common routes: a runc exploit (a CVE in the container runtime itself), or a misconfigured privileged container or mounted host filesystem/Docker socket that hands the attacker host access by design. Name two escape techniques and tell me, for one of them, whether it is a bug you patch or a configuration you should never have made.

mastery_questions: A container escape is the nightmare scenario of containerisation: an attacker who has compromised the inside of a container breaks out to the host itself — and because every container on that host shares the same kernel, escaping to the host can mean owning every other container too. Remember the core fact that makes this possible: a container is not a VM; it is an isolated process sharing the host's kernel, so a kernel vulnerability or a too-generous configuration is a door out. Two common routes: a runc exploit (a CVE in the container runtime itself), or a misconfigured privileged container or mounted host filesystem/Docker socket that hands the attacker host access by design. Name two escape techniques and tell me, for one of them, whether it is a bug you patch or a configuration you should never have made.

A privileged container (--privileged) is one that has been stripped of nearly all the isolation that makes containers safe — it gets almost all Linux capabilities, access to host devices, and effectively the keys to the host kernel. People reach for it because something did not work and --privileged made the error go away, which is exactly why it is so dangerous in production. Here is the distinction that trips people up: running as root inside a normal container is contained — that root is namespaced and limited; but --privileged removes the walls of the container itself, so the in-container root now has real power over the host. Explain that difference to me as if I had just added --privileged to fix a permissions error, and tell me what I should have done instead.

Kubernetes RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) governs who can do what in your cluster, and the most-confused pair is Role versus ClusterRole. A Role grants permissions within a single namespace — 'you can read pods, but only in the payments namespace'. A ClusterRole grants permissions across the whole cluster — 'you can read pods everywhere', or it covers cluster-scoped things like nodes that do not live in any namespace. The danger is over-using ClusterRoles or binding them too widely, because a ClusterRole bound to the wrong service account is a cluster-wide privilege the attacker will hunt for. Give me one scenario where a Role is the right choice and one where you genuinely need a ClusterRole — and explain the blast-radius difference if each is compromised.

A Kubernetes Network Policy is a firewall for pod-to-pod traffic — and the thing to internalise is that, by default, Kubernetes lets every pod talk to every other pod, so without policies your cluster is flat and an attacker who lands in one pod can reach them all. A policy lets you flip to default-deny and then explicitly allow only the connections you need. For the classic ask — deny all ingress to a namespace except from pods labelled app=frontend — your policy selects the target pods, sets policyTypes to Ingress, and defines one 'from' rule with a podSelector matching app=frontend. Sketch that policy for me, and then tell me the subtle thing beginners forget: what happens to traffic from pods that do not match, and why a default-deny posture changes your whole mental model.

The Kubernetes API server is the brain of the cluster — every command, every deployment, every secret read flows through it, and it is the single most valuable target in the whole system. If it is exposed to the internet with no authentication, you have not been hacked yet — you have simply published an admin console for your entire infrastructure, and that is precisely the 2018 Tesla story, where an open Kubernetes dashboard let attackers in to mine cryptocurrency on their cloud bill. Whoever reaches an unauthenticated API server can deploy pods, read every secret, and pivot to the underlying nodes. Tell me what an attacker does in the first five minutes after finding an open API server, and name the controls that should have stood between them and it.

common_mistakes: Running containers as root — containers should run as non-root users. Add 'USER nobody' to your Dockerfile.
Using --privileged in production — a privileged container has full access to the host. Only use it for specific tooling with awareness of the risk.
Not setting resource limits — a container without CPU/memory limits can starve other containers on the node (denial of service).
Leaving the Kubernetes dashboard exposed — it should require authentication and not be publicly accessible. Many clusters have it open by default.
Not scanning container images in CI — by the time an image reaches production, you should know every CVE in it and have accepted or mitigated each one.

weeks.title: DevSecOps — Security Throughout the SDLC
weeks.context:
DevSecOps integrates security into every phase of the software development lifecycle — not as a gate at the end, but as a continuous practice. The goal: find and fix security issues as early as possible, when they are cheapest to fix.

The DevSecOps toolchain has four layers: SAST (Static Application Security Testing — analysing source code for vulnerabilities without executing it), DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing — attacking a running app), SCA (Software Composition Analysis — finding vulnerable dependencies), and secrets scanning (finding leaked API keys, passwords).

This week you build a security-aware CI/CD pipeline that runs all four layers on every pull request. A developer should see security feedback in the same place they see test results — in their pull request, before merge.
topics: Shift-left security — what each stage should catch
SAST (Static Application Security Testing) — Semgrep, CodeQL, SonarQube
SCA (Software Composition Analysis) — Snyk, Dependabot, Renovate
Secret scanning — gitleaks, trufflehog, GitHub's built-in
IaC scanning — Checkov, tfsec, KICS
Container scanning — Trivy, Grype, Snyk Container
DAST (Dynamic) — OWASP ZAP in CI
PR-time feedback vs nightly scans — when each fits
tasks: Add Semgrep to one repo's CI; fix every finding
Enable Dependabot security updates on a repo with stale deps
Add gitleaks to your pre-commit hook; verify it blocks a test secret
Run Checkov against your Terraform; document findings
Add Trivy container scanning to your CI; fail on HIGH
weeks.project: Build a Full DevSecOps Pipeline. Take one project. Add: pre-commit (gitleaks, format), PR-CI (Semgrep, Trivy IaC, Trivy container, dependency audit), nightly DAST scan against staging. Each finding rated + triaged. Document the pipeline in DEVSECOPS.md. The bar: a contributor can't push insecure code by accident.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: SAST and DAST attack the same problem — finding vulnerabilities — from opposite ends. SAST (Static Application Security Testing) reads your source code without running it, so it is great at spotting code-level patterns like a SQL query built by string concatenation, a hardcoded secret, or unsafe deserialisation — and it can do this on every commit, before anything is deployed. DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing) ignores the code and attacks the running app from the outside like a real hacker, so it is great at finding things that only exist at runtime — authentication flaws, server misconfigurations, broken redirects — that SAST cannot see because they are not in the code. Each is blind where the other sees: SAST cannot tell if a vuln is actually exploitable, DAST cannot tell you which line to fix. Give me one vulnerability SAST catches that DAST misses, and one the reverse — and explain why neither alone is enough.

mastery_questions: SAST and DAST attack the same problem — finding vulnerabilities — from opposite ends. SAST (Static Application Security Testing) reads your source code without running it, so it is great at spotting code-level patterns like a SQL query built by string concatenation, a hardcoded secret, or unsafe deserialisation — and it can do this on every commit, before anything is deployed. DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing) ignores the code and attacks the running app from the outside like a real hacker, so it is great at finding things that only exist at runtime — authentication flaws, server misconfigurations, broken redirects — that SAST cannot see because they are not in the code. Each is blind where the other sees: SAST cannot tell if a vuln is actually exploitable, DAST cannot tell you which line to fix. Give me one vulnerability SAST catches that DAST misses, and one the reverse — and explain why neither alone is enough.

Software Composition Analysis (SCA) scans your dependencies — all the open-source packages you did not write but ship anyway — and flags the ones with known vulnerabilities (CVEs). Here is the judgement call that separates a junior from a senior: a tool screams 'CVE, CVSS 7.5!' on a library, but you discover your code never calls the vulnerable function in it. Do you drop everything? Not necessarily — a vulnerability you do not reach is not exploitable today, so you can often downgrade its urgency rather than triggering an emergency. But 'we do not call it today' can change with the next refactor, so you document the decision, suppress the alert with a reason, and re-evaluate on changes. Walk me through how you would decide whether that 7.5 is a 'fix tonight' or a 'fix next sprint', and what evidence backs your call.

Stopping secrets from reaching git is a layered problem, because relying on developers to 'just be careful' always fails eventually. The naive answer is a pre-commit hook (gitleaks/trufflehog) that scans before a commit lands — useful, but a hook lives on the developer's machine and can be skipped or missing. So you stack controls: server-side scanning in CI that blocks the merge regardless of local setup, push protection enabled at the platform (GitHub will reject a push containing a recognised secret), and — the real fix — making secrets unnecessary in code at all by using a secrets manager or short-lived credentials so there is nothing to leak. And critically: any secret that did hit a repo must be rotated, because git history is forever. Name three controls beyond the local hook, and tell me which one a determined-but-careless developer cannot bypass.

'Shift left' means moving security checks earlier in the timeline — left on the diagram that runs commit then build then test then deploy then production — so problems are caught when they are cheap instead of when they are catastrophic. The economics drive everything: a vulnerability caught in PR review costs minutes — the author fixes it in the same context they wrote it, before it ever ships. The same vulnerability found in production costs orders of magnitude more — incident response, emergency patching, possible breach, customer notification, reputational damage, and a developer who has long forgotten the code. That gap (often cited as 10x to 100x per stage) is the entire business case for DevSecOps. Tell me, for one concrete bug type, what catching it in PR costs versus catching it after a breach — and use that to argue why the security checks belong in CI, not a quarterly audit.

Let's make this concrete — design the security pipeline for a Node.js web app, stage by stage, and notice how each stage catches a different class of problem. At commit time, a pre-commit hook runs secret scanning and formatting. At PR/CI time, you run SAST (Semgrep) on the code, SCA (npm audit / Snyk) on dependencies, IaC scanning (Trivy/Checkov) on your Terraform, and container scanning on the built image — all failing the build before merge. Post-merge, you build and sign the image; against staging, you run a DAST scan (OWASP ZAP) on the live app; and nightly you re-scan for newly disclosed CVEs in dependencies you already shipped. The principle: each stage catches what the earlier ones structurally cannot. Walk me through your pipeline and, for each stage, name the one vulnerability class it exists to catch.

**Tools to install/configure this week:**

SAST:
```bash
# Semgrep (free, open-source)
pip install semgrep
semgrep --config=auto ./src
```

SCA (dependency scanning):
```bash
# npm audit (built-in)
npm audit
npm audit fix

# Snyk (free tier)
npm install -g snyk
snyk test
```

Secrets scanning:
```bash
# gitleaks
brew install gitleaks
gitleaks detect --source . --verbose
```

DAST (against running app):
```bash
# ZAP baseline scan
docker run -t owasp/zap2docker-stable zap-baseline.py -t http://your-app-url
```

**GitHub Actions security workflow (save this):**
```yaml
name: Security Scan
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  sast:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Semgrep SAST
        uses: returntocorp/semgrep-action@v1
        with:
          config: auto
  sca:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm audit --audit-level=high
  secrets:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - uses: gitleaks/gitleaks-action@v2
```
common_mistakes: Running security tools but ignoring the output — SAST findings that nobody acts on are worse than no SAST. Triage, assign, and track findings.
Treating all SAST findings as bugs — SAST has high false positive rates. Every finding needs human review before it becomes a bug.
Only scanning at release — scanning in CI on every PR catches issues before they accumulate. End-of-cycle security scans always find too much to fix.
Not managing the vulnerability backlog — SCA will find hundreds of outdated dependencies. Triage by exploitability and exposure, not just CVSS score.
Adding security gates that block deploys without team buy-in — security gates that block shipping create friction and get removed. Start with warnings, graduate to blocking only for Critical.

weeks.title: Threat Modelling — Designing Security Before Code
weeks.context:
Threat modelling is the practice of systematically identifying what can go wrong in a system before you build it. Done well, it shifts security from reactive (finding bugs after shipping) to proactive (designing them out before writing a line of code).

The most widely used methodology is STRIDE: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege. You apply STRIDE to a data flow diagram (DFD) of your system, identify threats at each trust boundary, and design mitigations.

This week you learn to draw DFDs, run STRIDE analysis, and produce a threat model document that engineers can act on. Threat modelling is a skill that makes you valuable at any seniority level — most teams do it poorly or not at all.
topics: Threat modelling methodologies — STRIDE, PASTA, LINDDUN
Data flow diagrams (DFDs) as the threat model substrate
Trust boundaries — where attackers live
STRIDE categories — Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Info disclosure, DoS, Elevation
Likelihood + impact rating
Mitigations as design choices, not afterthoughts
Lightweight threat modelling for sprint work
Tools — OWASP Threat Dragon, IriusRisk, hand-drawn
tasks: Read 'Threat Modeling: Designing for Security' chapters 1-4
Draw a DFD for one of your apps (use OWASP Threat Dragon or paper)
Apply STRIDE to each data flow; identify at least 10 threats
Rate each threat by likelihood + impact; pick the top 5 to mitigate
Design mitigations for each; verify in code

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Threat modelling starts with a picture, not a checklist — you draw a Data Flow Diagram (DFD) showing how data moves through your system, because you cannot defend what you cannot see. For a login flow — user then browser then web app then database — the interesting part is the trust boundary between the browser (which the attacker fully controls) and your web app (which you control); every byte crossing that line is suspect. Now apply STRIDE at that boundary: Spoofing (can someone impersonate the user? then need authentication), Tampering (can they alter the request in transit? then need TLS/integrity), Repudiation (can they deny acting? then need logging), Information disclosure (can they read others' data? then need authorisation), Denial of Service (can they flood login? then need rate limiting), Elevation of privilege (can a normal user become admin? then need access checks). Draw that DFD for me, mark the browser-to-app boundary, and give me the single most dangerous STRIDE threat at it and your mitigation.

mastery_questions: Threat modelling starts with a picture, not a checklist — you draw a Data Flow Diagram (DFD) showing how data moves through your system, because you cannot defend what you cannot see. For a login flow — user then browser then web app then database — the interesting part is the trust boundary between the browser (which the attacker fully controls) and your web app (which you control); every byte crossing that line is suspect. Now apply STRIDE at that boundary: Spoofing (can someone impersonate the user? then need authentication), Tampering (can they alter the request in transit? then need TLS/integrity), Repudiation (can they deny acting? then need logging), Information disclosure (can they read others' data? then need authorisation), Denial of Service (can they flood login? then need rate limiting), Elevation of privilege (can a normal user become admin? then need access checks). Draw that DFD for me, mark the browser-to-app boundary, and give me the single most dangerous STRIDE threat at it and your mitigation.

A trust boundary is any line in your system where the level of trust changes — where data or control passes from something you do not trust to something you do, or from one privilege level to another. It is the place attackers live, because it is where assumptions get violated. In a typical SaaS app the boundaries are everywhere once you look: the browser-to-server line (the user controls everything on their side), the server-to-database line, the boundary between your app and any third-party API you call, and the boundary between a regular user's session and an admin function. The skill is seeing them, because un-validated data crossing a boundary is the root of most vulnerabilities. Give me three trust boundaries in a SaaS app you know, and for one of them tell me what bad thing happens if you forget it is a boundary and trust the data crossing it.

STRIDE and the OWASP Top 10 are both vulnerability frameworks, but they answer different questions and you use them at different times. STRIDE is a design-time thinking tool — it is a set of six categories you apply to your architecture before you build, to systematically ask 'what could go wrong here?' and design defences in. The OWASP Top 10 is an awareness and testing list — the ten most common real-world web vulnerability classes, useful as a checklist when you are reviewing or testing an app that already exists. One is proactive and architectural; the other is a reactive, prioritised 'watch out for these'. Tell me which you would reach for when someone hands you a whiteboard and an idea, and which when they hand you a running app and a deadline — and why mixing them up wastes effort.

PASTA (Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis) is a heavier, seven-stage threat-modelling methodology that differs from STRIDE in one key way: it is risk- and attacker-centric rather than checklist-centric. Where STRIDE asks 'which of these six categories apply to each component?', PASTA starts from business objectives, builds an attacker's-eye view, and walks through simulating realistic attacks to see which threats actually matter to this business — so it produces a risk-prioritised output, not just a list of possible threats. The trade-off is obvious: PASTA is far more thorough and far more expensive in time, so it fits high-stakes systems, while STRIDE fits a sprint. Tell me what PASTA gives you that STRIDE does not, and on what kind of project the extra cost is actually worth it.

When a product manager says 'we do not have time for threat modelling', they are making an implicit bet that the cost of skipping it is zero — and your job is to make that hidden cost visible. Do not argue in principle; argue in numbers: a threat-modelling session for a feature costs maybe a few engineer-hours up front, while a single design-level vulnerability that ships can cost an emergency fix, an incident, possible breach disclosure, and the brutal multiplier that architectural flaws found in production often require re-architecting, not a one-line patch. Frame it as the shift-left economics they already accept for bugs. Give me the actual sentence you would say to that PM to reframe threat modelling as the cheap option, and one number you would put on the table.

weeks.pre_flight:
**Threat modelling tools (free):**
- OWASP Threat Dragon: https://owasp.org/www-project-threat-dragon/ (browser-based DFD tool)
- Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool: https://aka.ms/threatmodelingtool (Windows only)
- Draw.io: just use shapes to draw DFDs manually

**The 4 questions of threat modelling (Adam Shostack):**
1. What are we building? (DFD)
2. What can go wrong? (STRIDE)
3. What are we going to do about it? (mitigations)
4. Did we do a good enough job? (review)

**STRIDE categories:**
```
Spoofing        → Authentication controls
Tampering       → Integrity controls (checksums, MACs, signatures)
Repudiation     → Audit logging, non-repudiation
Information Disclosure → Confidentiality controls (encryption, access control)
Denial of Service → Availability controls (rate limiting, redundancy)
Elevation of Privilege → Authorisation controls (RBAC, least privilege)
```

**Data flow diagram elements:**
- Rectangle: external entity (user, third-party service)
- Circle/oval: process (your application code)
- Parallel lines: data store (database, file system, cache)
- Arrow: data flow
- Dashed line: trust boundary
common_mistakes: Making the DFD too granular — you don't need every function call. One process per logical component (auth service, payment service) is the right level.
Only modelling the happy path — threat modelling must include error paths, retry logic, admin flows, and third-party integrations.
Not assigning mitigations to owners — a threat model with no owner for each mitigation sits in a document forever. Every finding needs an owner and a deadline.
Treating threat modelling as a one-time exercise — systems change. Re-run threat modelling whenever you add a new trust boundary, data store, or external integration.
Confusing threats with vulnerabilities — a threat is 'attacker spoofs user identity', a vulnerability is 'no MFA on admin accounts'. Threats are abstract; vulnerabilities are specific.
weeks.debug_help:
**OWASP Threat Dragon won't load DFD?**
- Use the browser-based version at: https://www.threatdragon.com/
- Export your DFD as JSON for version control

**STRIDE analysis feeling mechanical?**
Apply these questions at each trust boundary:
1. Could an attacker pretend to be someone they're not? (Spoofing)
2. Could an attacker modify data in transit? (Tampering)
3. Could an action be denied later? (Repudiation)
4. Could an attacker read data they should not? (Information Disclosure)
5. Could an attacker make the system unavailable? (DoS)
6. Could an attacker gain more permissions than they have? (EoP)

**Threat model template:**
```markdown
## Threat: [Name]
STRIDE category: Tampering
Affected component: Payment API
Description: An attacker in a MITM position modifies the transaction amount in transit.
Likelihood: Low (HTTPS in use)
Impact: High (financial loss)
Mitigation: Enforce TLS 1.2+, certificate pinning on mobile client, request signing.
Owner: Backend team
Due date: Q1 2026
```

weeks.title: Application Security — SAST, DAST, IAST
weeks.context:
Application security (AppSec) is the discipline of making software secure. This week you go deeper into the testing methodologies: SAST (static analysis of code), DAST (dynamic testing of a running app), and IAST (instrumentation inside a running app that observes its own behaviour).

Each has different coverage: SAST finds code-level issues without running the app (good for injection, hardcoded secrets, insecure patterns); DAST attacks the running app from outside (good for auth issues, injection, misconfigurations); IAST sits inside the app and observes data flows at runtime (best coverage, highest complexity).

You also learn code review for security this week — how to manually review a pull request and identify security issues that no automated tool would catch, like broken business logic.
topics: Secure coding patterns — input validation, output encoding, parameterised everything
Manual code review — what to look for, where bugs hide
