items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You already know SAST (reads code, runs early) and DAST (attacks the running app from outside) — IAST (Interactive Application Security Testing) is the third approach that sits inside the running application via instrumentation, watching its actual data flows from within as the app handles real requests. Picture where each lives on the build then test then deploy timeline: SAST runs at the code/CI stage on the source; DAST runs at the test/staging stage against a deployed instance from the outside; IAST runs during testing too but from inside the running app, so it sees both the request and the line of code that handled it. That inside view gives IAST the best accuracy — it can confirm a vuln is real and point to the code — at the cost of complexity and runtime overhead. Draw me the SDLC and place all three, and tell me why IAST's position lets it cut the false positives that plague SAST.

mastery_questions: You already know SAST (reads code, runs early) and DAST (attacks the running app from outside) — IAST (Interactive Application Security Testing) is the third approach that sits inside the running application via instrumentation, watching its actual data flows from within as the app handles real requests. Picture where each lives on the build then test then deploy timeline: SAST runs at the code/CI stage on the source; DAST runs at the test/staging stage against a deployed instance from the outside; IAST runs during testing too but from inside the running app, so it sees both the request and the line of code that handled it. That inside view gives IAST the best accuracy — it can confirm a vuln is real and point to the code — at the cost of complexity and runtime overhead. Draw me the SDLC and place all three, and tell me why IAST's position lets it cut the false positives that plague SAST.

You are reviewing a pull request and you see a SQL query built with string concatenation — user input glued directly into the query text. Stop: this is SQL injection waiting to happen, because the database cannot tell your intended query structure from data the user smuggled in. The exact change you request is parameterised queries (prepared statements): the query text with placeholders is sent to the database separately from the values, so the user's input is always treated as data, never as executable SQL — there is no string for them to break out of. Do not accept 'I will just escape the input' as a fix; escaping is error-prone and parameterisation is the actual solution. Write me the before-and-after for one query, and explain to the PR author why parameterisation defeats injection at a structural level, not just by filtering bad characters.

In security testing, a false positive is the tool crying wolf — it flags something as vulnerable that actually is not — while a false negative is the silent killer — a real vulnerability the tool failed to flag, so you ship it believing you are safe. Both are costly but asymmetrically: false positives waste analyst time and, worse, breed alert fatigue until people start ignoring the tool; false negatives give you false confidence about a real hole. In a security context the false negative is usually the more dangerous, because a noisy tool annoys you but a blind spot gets you breached — though enough false positives can cause false negatives by making humans tune out. Tell me which you would rather tolerate on a tool guarding your auth code, and defend the trade-off you are making.

IAST works by instrumenting the application — inserting sensors into the running code (via an agent, hooks, or bytecode modification) so it can watch data flow through the app from the inside as it processes real requests during testing. Contrast it with DAST: DAST is a blind attacker outside the box, throwing payloads and inferring vulnerabilities from responses — it has no idea what happened internally, so it both misses things and cannot tell you where to fix. IAST sees the payload arrive and watches it flow into, say, a database call without sanitisation — so it confirms the vuln with high accuracy and points at the exact code path. The cost is that you have to run an agent inside your app, with performance and deployment complexity. Explain how that inside view makes IAST both more accurate and lower-false-positive than DAST, and one situation where you would still prefer DAST.

A broken business logic vulnerability is a flaw in what your application is allowed to do, not in how it is coded — the code is perfectly 'secure' (no injection, no XSS), but the rules it enforces are wrong. Classic example: an e-commerce checkout where you can apply the same single-use discount code a hundred times, or change the quantity to a negative number and get credited, or skip from step 1 to step 3 and bypass payment. SAST and DAST both miss these because there is no malformed input and no insecure pattern — every request is technically valid; only a human who understands the intended business rules can see that the app is being abused within the rules. Give me a business-logic flaw in your own URL shortener or checkout, and explain exactly why no automated scanner would ever catch it.

**Code review checklist (save this):**

common_mistakes: Running SAST and treating the output as ground truth — SAST tools are wrong often. Every finding needs manual confirmation.
Only running DAST against the happy path — DAST needs to be authenticated and needs to cover every application feature, not just the home page.
Skipping manual code review in favour of automated tools — tools miss business logic bugs, race conditions, and architectural flaws. Human review is irreplaceable.
Not integrating tools into CI — security tools run once at audit time are not security. They must run continuously on every change.
Fixing SAST findings without understanding why they are vulnerabilities — developers who don't understand the vulnerability will recreate it in a different form.

weeks.title: Software Supply Chain Security
weeks.context:
The SolarWinds attack in 2020 compromised 18,000 organisations by injecting malicious code into a trusted software update. The Log4Shell vulnerability in 2021 affected millions of apps because they all used the same dependency. Supply chain security is now one of the top priorities in enterprise security.

Your application's attack surface is not just your code — it includes every npm package, Docker base image, CI/CD tool, and cloud provider you depend on. An attacker who compromises any of these can compromise you.

This week you learn: dependency pinning and verification, SBOM (Software Bill of Materials), signed commits and releases, provenance and reproducible builds, and how to use tools like Sigstore/cosign to cryptographically verify the software you consume.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: A software supply chain attack compromises you not by attacking your code, but by poisoning something you trust and pull in — a dependency, a base image, a build tool, an update. It is devastating because it inherits your trust: you invited the malicious code in through the front door. SolarWinds in 2020 is the canonical case — attackers breached SolarWinds' build pipeline and slipped malicious code into a legitimate, digitally-signed update of their Orion product, which then auto-deployed to roughly 18,000 customers who had every reason to trust it. The lesson is that 'we secured our code' is not enough when your attack surface includes everyone you depend on. Describe the SolarWinds mechanism back to me in three sentences, and tell me which link in your own build chain a SolarWinds-style attacker would target.

mastery_questions: A software supply chain attack compromises you not by attacking your code, but by poisoning something you trust and pull in — a dependency, a base image, a build tool, an update. It is devastating because it inherits your trust: you invited the malicious code in through the front door. SolarWinds in 2020 is the canonical case — attackers breached SolarWinds' build pipeline and slipped malicious code into a legitimate, digitally-signed update of their Orion product, which then auto-deployed to roughly 18,000 customers who had every reason to trust it. The lesson is that 'we secured our code' is not enough when your attack surface includes everyone you depend on. Describe the SolarWinds mechanism back to me in three sentences, and tell me which link in your own build chain a SolarWinds-style attacker would target.

An SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) is a complete, machine-readable inventory of every component in your software — every dependency, version, and license — like the ingredients list on food packaging. The reason it suddenly matters: when Log4Shell hit, the urgent question across the planet was 'do we even use Log4j, and where?' — and companies without an SBOM spent days manually hunting while attackers exploited the window. With an SBOM you answer in minutes. It is increasingly required — governments and enterprises demand it before they will run your software — and the common formats are SPDX and CycloneDX. Tell me who needs your SBOM and why, and walk me through how having one turns a 'panic for days' CVE response into a 'grep for minutes' one.

Dependency pinning and integrity checking sound similar but defend against different attacks, and you need both. Pinning means specifying an exact version (lodash 4.17.21, not a caret range) so your build is reproducible and a malicious new release cannot silently slip in when you next install. But pinning a version number alone does not help if an attacker replaces the contents of that exact version on the registry — so integrity checking adds a cryptographic hash (the lock file's integrity field) that verifies the package's contents match what you expect, byte for byte. Pinning controls which version; integrity controls that the bytes are genuine. Give me one attack pinning stops, one attack only integrity checking stops, and explain why a lock file gives you both.

Sigstore (via its cosign tool) lets you cryptographically sign software — like container images — so consumers can verify it genuinely came from you and was not tampered with. Its clever twist is keyless signing: instead of you guarding a long-lived private key that could leak, cosign uses your existing identity (an OIDC login — your Google/GitHub account) to obtain a short-lived certificate, signs with that, and records the signature in a public transparency log. So there is no secret key to steal. But be precise about what a signature proves: it proves who signed it and that the artefact has not changed since — it does not prove the code is safe or bug-free. Explain keyless signing back to me, and tell me the dangerous mistake of believing 'signed' means 'secure'.

Typosquatting in a package registry is when an attacker publishes a malicious package with a name almost identical to a popular one, betting that someone will fat-finger the install — python-requests instead of requests, electorn instead of electron, lodahs instead of lodash. The moment a developer (or a CI pipeline) installs the wrong name, the attacker's code runs with whatever permissions the build has — and it often quietly does its job plus the malicious one so nobody notices. It is a close cousin of dependency confusion, where a public package shadows a company's private one. Give me a plausible typosquat of a package you actually use, and tell me one control that stops a typo'd install from ever executing malicious code in your pipeline.

weeks.pre_flight:
**SBOM generation:**
```bash
# CycloneDX for npm
npm install -g @cyclonedx/cyclonedx-npm
cyclonedx-npm --output-file sbom.json

# Syft for container images
brew install syft
syft nginx:latest -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.json
```

**Sigstore/cosign — signing and verifying container images:**
```bash
brew install cosign
# Sign an image (requires OIDC token)
cosign sign --key cosign.key your-registry/your-image:tag
# Verify a signed image
cosign verify --key cosign.pub your-registry/your-image:tag
```

**Dependency pinning in package.json:**
```json
{
  "dependencies": {
    "express": "4.18.2"
  }
}
```
Pinning to exact versions + using npm ci (not npm install) in CI ensures reproducibility.

**GitHub commit signing:**
```bash
git config --global commit.gpgsign true
git config --global user.signingkey YOUR_GPG_KEY_ID
# Or use SSH signing (simpler)
git config --global gpg.format ssh
git config --global user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
```
common_mistakes: Using ^ or ~ version specifiers in production — these allow minor/patch version float. A malicious patch release can get pulled automatically.
Not locking your lock files in CI — run npm ci (not npm install) in CI. npm ci requires package-lock.json and fails if it is inconsistent.
Trusting popular packages without scrutiny — high download counts do not mean secure. Popular packages are high-value targets for supply chain attacks.
Not auditing transitive dependencies — a direct dependency that is secure can depend on a transitive dependency that is not. SCA tools check the full tree.
Not rotating build tool credentials — CI secrets (npm tokens, Docker Hub credentials) are high-value targets. Rotate them regularly and scope them minimally.

weeks.title: Compliance — SOC2, ISO27001, GDPR
weeks.context:
Compliance is how organisations demonstrate their security posture to customers, regulators, and auditors. It is not security itself — a fully compliant organisation can still be breached. But compliance frameworks (SOC 2, ISO 27001, GDPR) encode security best practices that, when implemented honestly, meaningfully reduce risk.

For a security engineer, understanding compliance is essential because it translates business requirements into technical controls. An enterprise customer saying 'do you have SOC 2 Type II?' means 'can you prove your security controls have operated continuously for at least 6 months?'

This week you learn the major frameworks, how to map your technical controls to compliance requirements, and how to prepare for and support an audit.

GDPR — the principles, the big penalties, the consent question
PCI DSS — if you touch credit cards
HIPAA — if you touch US health data

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: SOC 2 is an audit that proves your security controls to enterprise customers, and the Type I versus Type II distinction is about time. A Type I report says 'on this single date, the auditor confirmed these controls were designed correctly' — a snapshot, a photograph. A Type II report says 'over a period of at least six months, the auditor confirmed these controls actually operated continuously and effectively' — a video, not a photo. Enterprise customers almost always want Type II, because anyone can look secure for one day; what they are buying is proof you stay secure. Tell me which one a serious enterprise buyer demands before signing, and why the snapshot is so much weaker than the period-of-time evidence.

mastery_questions: SOC 2 is an audit that proves your security controls to enterprise customers, and the Type I versus Type II distinction is about time. A Type I report says 'on this single date, the auditor confirmed these controls were designed correctly' — a snapshot, a photograph. A Type II report says 'over a period of at least six months, the auditor confirmed these controls actually operated continuously and effectively' — a video, not a photo. Enterprise customers almost always want Type II, because anyone can look secure for one day; what they are buying is proof you stay secure. Tell me which one a serious enterprise buyer demands before signing, and why the snapshot is so much weaker than the period-of-time evidence.

A user emailing 'delete my data' is invoking their GDPR right to erasure (the 'right to be forgotten'), and your response is both a legal obligation and an engineering problem. Legally, you generally must act without undue delay and within one month, you must actually erase their personal data (not just deactivate the account), and that includes data in backups, logs, and anywhere it has been copied or shared with processors — though there are lawful exceptions where you must retain some data (e.g. financial records for tax law). The engineering trap is that 'delete the row' rarely covers it — personal data leaks into analytics, third-party tools, and backups. Walk me through what you would actually do and in what timeframe, and name the one place personal data hides that teams forget to delete.

SOC 2 is organised around Trust Service Criteria (TSC) — Security, Availability, Confidentiality, Processing Integrity, and Privacy — and a core skill is mapping a concrete technical control to the criterion (and underlying requirement) it satisfies, because that mapping is what an auditor checks. The point is not memorising categories; it is seeing that a control is evidence for a promise you are making. So: MFA maps to Security (logical access control — proving only authorised people get in); backup encryption maps to Confidentiality (protecting data at rest); access logs map to Security/monitoring (you can detect and investigate access); security training maps to the Security control environment (your people are a control too). Map those four for me, and for one of them tell me the exact evidence you would hand an auditor to prove it is not just on paper.

A RACI chart assigns four roles to every task or control — Responsible (does the work), Accountable (owns the outcome, the single neck on the line), Consulted (gives input), Informed (kept in the loop) — and in compliance it exists to kill the deadliest phrase in security: 'I thought someone else was handling that'. Every control needs a named owner because an unowned control silently rots — nobody patches it, nobody reviews the logs, nobody renews the cert — and at audit time 'everyone and no one' owns it. The 'A' is the crucial one: exactly one person is accountable, so there is never ambiguity about who answers when it fails. Take one control from your SOC2-readiness doc and assign its RACI — and tell me why having two 'Accountable' people is as broken as having zero.

When a startup moves into enterprise sales, the question 'which compliance framework first?' usually has a clear answer driven by your buyers, not your preferences — and that is the lesson: compliance is a sales enabler, so you pursue what unblocks revenue. For a US-market B2B SaaS, that is almost always SOC 2 (Type II), because it is the report North American enterprise procurement teams ask for by name before they will sign. ISO 27001 matters more for international/European deals; GDPR is a legal obligation triggered by handling EU personal data, not a 'choice'; PCI DSS only if you touch card data. The skill is matching the framework to where your deals are stalling. Tell me which framework you would pursue first for a US-focused SaaS and exactly which business signal would change your answer.

**Framework summaries to read:**

SOC 2 (US, for SaaS):
- 5 Trust Service Criteria: Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, Privacy
- Type I: controls exist at a point in time
- Type II: controls operated effectively for 6-12 months
- Common controls: access management, encryption, logging, vulnerability management

ISO 27001 (international):
- Information Security Management System (ISMS)
- 93 controls across 4 themes: Organisational, People, Physical, Technological
- Requires annual audit + certification body

GDPR (EU, for any company handling EU personal data):
- Lawful basis for processing
- Data subject rights (access, deletion, portability)
- Privacy by design and default
- 72-hour breach notification to regulator
- DPA (Data Processing Agreement) with sub-processors

**Free resource:**
SOC 2 Academy by Drata: https://drata.com/resources/soc-2-academy
Vanta's compliance guides: https://www.vanta.com/resources
common_mistakes: Treating compliance as the goal instead of security — passing an audit by ticking boxes does not protect your users. Implement controls because they work, not because they are required.
Not having a written policy for every control — compliance auditors ask for evidence. A technical control without a documented policy is an audit finding.
Scoping SOC 2 too broadly — only the systems that handle customer data are in scope. Over-scoping makes audits expensive and long.
Ignoring vendor compliance — your subprocessors must also be compliant. Review their SOC 2 reports before signing contracts.
Not logging compliance events — access grants, privilege escalation, configuration changes, and security events must be logged in a tamper-proof system.

weeks.title: Identity, Access, and Zero Trust
weeks.context:
Zero Trust is the modern security architecture principle: never trust, always verify. It rejects the old perimeter model (trust everything inside the network) and replaces it with: authenticate and authorise every request, every time, regardless of network location.

The practical implementation of Zero Trust involves: strong identity verification (MFA, hardware keys), device health checks, least-privilege access, micro-segmentation (network policies that limit lateral movement), and continuous monitoring. Every access decision is made based on identity + device health + context, not IP address.

This week you learn Zero Trust architecture principles, how to implement them with tools like Tailscale (mesh VPN), Cloudflare Access (identity-aware proxy), and how to design access control systems that are both secure and usable.
topics: SSO — SAML vs OAuth vs OIDC, what each fits
Identity providers — Okta, Google Workspace, Microsoft Entra, Authentik
Multi-factor — TOTP, push, WebAuthn / passkeys (the gold standard)
Conditional access — country, device, time-of-day policies
Just-in-time access — temporary elevation, why daily admin is broken
Service-to-service auth — mTLS, SPIFFE, workload identity
Zero Trust Architecture — NIST SP 800-207
Google BeyondCorp + Cloudflare Zero Trust — real implementations

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Zero Trust's slogan 'never trust, always verify' is best understood by contrast with the model it replaced. The old perimeter model worked like a castle: a hard wall (the firewall) around the network, and everything inside was trusted — so once an attacker breached the wall (one phished laptop), they could move freely, because the inside was a soft, trusting interior. Zero Trust throws out 'inside means trusted': every request is authenticated and authorised individually, every time, based on identity plus device health plus context, regardless of whether it comes from the office network or a cafe. Network location stops being a credential. Explain to me why the castle model fails the moment one device inside is compromised, and what Zero Trust does differently that contains that same compromised device.

mastery_questions: Zero Trust's slogan 'never trust, always verify' is best understood by contrast with the model it replaced. The old perimeter model worked like a castle: a hard wall (the firewall) around the network, and everything inside was trusted — so once an attacker breached the wall (one phished laptop), they could move freely, because the inside was a soft, trusting interior. Zero Trust throws out 'inside means trusted': every request is authenticated and authorised individually, every time, based on identity plus device health plus context, regardless of whether it comes from the office network or a cafe. Network location stops being a credential. Explain to me why the castle model fails the moment one device inside is compromised, and what Zero Trust does differently that contains that same compromised device.

Authentication and authorisation are constantly muddled, but they answer two different questions: authentication (authn) asks 'who are you?' and proves identity (password, passkey, MFA); authorisation (authz) asks 'what are you allowed to do?' and enforces permissions. The clearest way to see the difference is to watch each fail independently. An authn failure: an attacker steals a valid session token and is now authenticated as you — the system is sure who they are, and it is wrong. An authz failure: a properly logged-in, correctly-authenticated normal user changes a URL from account/123 to account/124 and sees someone else's data — authn worked perfectly; authorisation did not check ownership (that is IDOR). Give me one concrete example of each failing on its own, and explain why fixing one does nothing for the other.

SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) is a protocol that enables Single Sign-On: instead of every app holding your password, they all trust a central Identity Provider (IdP), and when you log in to the IdP once it issues a signed XML 'assertion' vouching for you, which the app accepts — so one login unlocks many apps and there is one place to disable a departing employee. OIDC (OpenID Connect) does the same job but is built on modern OAuth 2.0 with JSON/JWT instead of XML, and is friendlier to mobile apps and APIs. So when do you still choose SAML? When you are integrating with established enterprise systems and corporate IdPs that speak SAML natively — it remains the lingua franca of B2B/workforce SSO. Explain how SAML delivers SSO step by step, and give me the situation where you would pick it over the newer OIDC.

Cloudflare Access is an identity-aware proxy — it implements Zero Trust for an internal web app by sitting in front of it so that no request reaches the app until the user has proven who they are and passed your policies. The flow: a user hits your internal tool's URL, Cloudflare intercepts, sees no valid session, and redirects them to log in via your identity provider (Google, Okta, etc.) plus any conditions you set (MFA, allowed country, device posture); only on success does Cloudflare mint a session and forward the request to the app. The app itself no longer needs a VPN in front of it or its own login — access is decided at the edge on identity, not network location. Walk me through that access flow end to end, and tell me what is no longer needed (and why that is the Zero Trust win) once Access is in front.

RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) grants permissions based on a user's role — 'editors can publish, viewers can read' — which is simple and scales well when access cleanly follows job function. ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control) decides based on attributes of the user, resource, and context evaluated at request time — 'allow if user.department equals document.department AND time is business hours AND user.country equals resource.region'. You need ABAC when roles alone explode: imagine a global company where a manager should see salaries only for their own department, only from a corporate device, only in their region — encoding every combination as a separate role becomes thousands of roles, while ABAC expresses it as one policy over attributes. Give me a scenario where RBAC forces a role explosion, and rewrite it as a single ABAC rule to show why attributes win there.

weeks.pre_flight:
**Zero Trust tools (free tier or open-source):**

Tailscale (mesh VPN, free for personal use):
```bash
# Install
curl -fsSL https://tailscale.com/install.sh | sh
sudo tailscale up
# Every device gets a Tailscale IP, accessible from anywhere
```

Cloudflare Access (Zero Trust proxy, free tier):
- Protects internal apps with identity verification
- Dashboard at: https://one.dash.cloudflare.com/

HashiCorp Vault (secrets management with identity-based access):
```bash
docker run --rm -p 8200:8200 --cap-add=IPC_LOCK vault server -dev
export VAULT_ADDR='http://127.0.0.1:8200'
vault status
```

**Zero Trust principles (NIST SP 800-207):**
1. All data sources and computing services are resources
2. All communication is secured regardless of network location
3. Access to individual resources is granted per-session
4. Access is determined by dynamic policy
5. No device is inherently trusted
6. All resource authentication and authorization is dynamic
7. Collect data to improve security posture
common_mistakes: Treating VPN as Zero Trust — a VPN places a user on the internal network. Zero Trust requires per-resource authentication even on the internal network. They are different things.
Over-relying on passwords — passwords are not strong authentication. MFA is the minimum; hardware keys (FIDO2/WebAuthn) are better for privileged access.
Broad group membership instead of least privilege — users accumulate permissions over time. Regular access reviews remove permissions that are no longer needed.
Not auditing service account permissions — service accounts often have wider access than needed and are rarely rotated. Treat them like privileged human accounts.
Implementing Zero Trust in one layer only — network-level Zero Trust without application-level authorisation is incomplete. Both layers must verify identity.
weeks.debug_help:
**Tailscale device not appearing in admin console?**
```bash
# Re-authenticate the device
sudo tailscale up --reset
# Check Tailscale status
tailscale status
```

**Cloudflare Access blocking legitimate users?**
- Check Access policies — are they set to 'Allow' or 'Block'?
- Review Access logs in the Cloudflare dashboard
- Test with the bypass rule for specific email domains during setup

**Vault not accepting token?**
```bash
# Check token validity
vault token lookup
# Re-login
vault login token=<your-token>
# List auth methods
vault auth list
```

weeks.title: Forensics and Malware Analysis Basics
weeks.context:
Digital forensics is the practice of recovering and analysing evidence from digital systems. Malware analysis is the reverse-engineering of malicious software to understand how it works. Together, they form the investigative backbone of incident response — you need both to answer "what happened, how, and what did the attacker do?"

Static analysis: examine a file without running it (strings, file type, hash, PE headers, disassembly). Dynamic analysis: run the malware in an isolated sandbox and observe what it does (network connections, file writes, registry changes, process creation). You start with static analysis for safety — you never run unknown malware on your own machine.

This week you learn basic forensics workflows, how to use ANY.RUN or Cuckoo for sandboxed malware analysis, and how to use Volatility for memory forensics. You also learn the basics of the Windows PE format — understanding the format helps you detect packed or obfuscated malware.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Static and dynamic analysis are the two halves of examining a suspect file, and the order matters for your safety. Static analysis examines the file without running it — you look at its strings, file type, hashes, headers, and disassembly to learn what it might do. Dynamic analysis runs it in an isolated sandbox and watches what it actually does — network connections, files written, registry changes, processes spawned. You always start static, for one blunt reason: you never execute unknown malware until you know something about it, because running it is exactly what the attacker wants, and a sandbox escape or a missed network call could infect your real environment. Tell me three things static analysis reveals before you would ever consider running the sample, and what dynamic analysis adds that static can never tell you.

mastery_questions: Static and dynamic analysis are the two halves of examining a suspect file, and the order matters for your safety. Static analysis examines the file without running it — you look at its strings, file type, hashes, headers, and disassembly to learn what it might do. Dynamic analysis runs it in an isolated sandbox and watches what it actually does — network connections, files written, registry changes, processes spawned. You always start static, for one blunt reason: you never execute unknown malware until you know something about it, because running it is exactly what the attacker wants, and a sandbox escape or a missed network call could infect your real environment. Tell me three things static analysis reveals before you would ever consider running the sample, and what dynamic analysis adds that static can never tell you.

A user forwards you a suspicious .docx — and the cardinal rule is you do not double-click it, because modern document attacks fire on open (malicious macros, embedded objects, exploit payloads). Your triage stays static and safe: first hash the file and check the hash against threat-intel services like VirusTotal to see if it is already known-bad; inspect the file's true type (a .docx is really a ZIP — you can unzip it and look inside without Word); examine the embedded macro/VBA code and any external relationships or URLs it tries to reach; and detonate it only in an isolated sandbox (ANY.RUN), never your own machine. The whole point is to learn its intent without ever giving it a chance to run on a system that matters. Walk me through your first checks on that file, in order, and explain why each one is safe.

A PE (Portable Executable) is the file format for Windows executables and DLLs — the .exe and .dll files — and understanding its structure is what lets you spot malware before you run it. It begins with headers (the old DOS stub, then the PE header describing the file) and is divided into sections, each with a job: .text holds the executable code, .data holds initialised global variables, .rdata holds read-only data like strings and the import table, and .rsrc holds resources like icons and embedded files. The import table is a goldmine — it lists which Windows API functions the program calls, so a binary importing crypto and network and process-injection APIs tells a story before you have run a single instruction. Name the sections and what each holds, and tell me what the import table alone might reveal about a sample's intent.

A running process lives in memory, and that memory is full of evidence that vanishes the instant the machine powers off — which is why memory forensics with a tool like Volatility is so valuable in incident response. From a memory dump you can recover the process tree (what spawned what — winword.exe spawning powershell.exe is a red flag), the network connections each process held open (the C2 address an attacker forgot to hide), command-line arguments, loaded DLLs and injected code, and even decrypted data and credentials that only exist in plaintext while running. The big idea: malware that is careful to leave nothing on disk still has to exist in memory to run. Tell me three artefacts you would pull from a memory dump to investigate a suspected compromise, and why each is something you could not get from the disk alone.

Packed malware is malware that has been compressed or encrypted and wrapped in a small stub of code that unpacks the real payload into memory at runtime — attackers do this to defeat static analysis and signature detection, because on disk the malicious code is scrambled and unreadable. The tells are detectable, though: a packed binary often has very high entropy (its bytes look random, like compressed/encrypted data), unusually few readable strings, tiny import tables, and section names like UPX0/UPX1. A tool like Detect It Easy (DiE), PEiD, or simply checking section entropy will flag it. Explain why high entropy is the giveaway, and tell me what packing forces an analyst to do next that static analysis alone cannot accomplish.

weeks.pre_flight:
**Static analysis tools:**
```bash
# strings — extract readable strings from a binary
strings suspicious.exe | grep -E "(http|cmd|powershell|reg)"

# file — identify file type regardless of extension
file suspicious.exe

# xxd — hex dump
xxd suspicious.exe | head -20

# sha256sum — compute hash for IOC lookup
sha256sum suspicious.exe
```

**Dynamic analysis (sandboxes — DO NOT run malware locally):**
- ANY.RUN: https://app.any.run/ (free tier, interactive sandbox)
- Hybrid Analysis: https://www.hybrid-analysis.com/ (free)
- Joe Sandbox Cloud Basic: https://www.joesandbox.com/

**Volatility 3 (memory forensics):**
```bash
pip install volatility3
# Download a test memory image
# https://github.com/volatilityfoundation/volatility/wiki/Memory-Samples

# List processes
vol -f memory.dmp windows.pslist
# Network connections
vol -f memory.dmp windows.netstat
# Command line arguments
vol -f memory.dmp windows.cmdline
# Dump a suspicious process
vol -f memory.dmp windows.dumpfiles --pid 1234
```
common_mistakes: Running unknown malware on your personal machine — always use an isolated VM or an online sandbox. Assume any suspicious file is live malware.
Trusting sandbox results without question — sophisticated malware detects sandbox environments and behaves differently. Static analysis is always needed too.
Not computing hashes before analysis — always hash the file first. The hash is your IOC and proves the file has not changed during your analysis.
Not preserving the original file — analysis can modify files. Work on a copy and preserve the original with documented chain of custody.
Missing the strings output — malware often contains readable strings: C2 URLs, mutex names, hardcoded paths. Strings is the first and fastest analysis step.
weeks.debug_help:
**Volatility can't identify the OS profile?**
```bash
# Volatility 3 auto-detects — if it fails, check the image is a full memory dump
# For Windows: the memory image must include the kernel
vol -f memory.dmp windows.info

# For Linux memory images
vol -f memory.dmp linux.pslist
```

**strings output too noisy?**
```bash
# Filter for URLs
strings suspicious.exe | grep -E "https?://"
# Filter for IPs
strings suspicious.exe | grep -E " ([0-9]{1,3}.){3}[0-9]{1,3} "
# Filter for registry keys
strings suspicious.exe | grep -i "HKEY"
```

**ANY.RUN free tier limitations?**
- Files up to 100MB
- 60 seconds execution time on free tier
- Use Hybrid Analysis for longer analysis

weeks.title: Tabletop Exercises and Red Teaming
weeks.context:
A tabletop exercise is a structured discussion where a team works through a simulated security incident. No systems are touched — it is a meeting. The value is in discovering gaps in your response process, communication chains, and decision-making before a real incident happens.

Red teaming is an adversarial simulation where a skilled team tries to compromise an organisation's defences using real attack techniques, with full scope and duration (days to weeks, not hours). Red team engagements are distinct from pentests: pentests find as many vulnerabilities as possible; red teams test whether defenders can detect and respond to a realistic attack.

This week you learn to run a basic tabletop exercise, understand the structure of a red team engagement, and learn about adversary simulation frameworks (Atomic Red Team, CALDERA) that let you safely simulate specific ATT&CK techniques in your own lab.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: These three exercises test your defences at very different costs and depths. A tabletop exercise is a meeting — no systems are touched; the team talks through a simulated incident to find gaps in process, communication, and decision-making ('who calls legal? who decides to pull the plug?'). A red team engagement is the opposite extreme — a skilled adversarial team actually attacks your live environment over days or weeks, with real techniques, to test whether your defenders detect and respond. A purple team sits in between and collaborative: red and blue work together in real time, the attacker runs a technique and the defender immediately checks 'did we see that?', tuning detections on the spot. Lay out the three for me on a scale of cost and realism, and tell me which one you would run first in an org that has never tested its defences, and why.

mastery_questions: These three exercises test your defences at very different costs and depths. A tabletop exercise is a meeting — no systems are touched; the team talks through a simulated incident to find gaps in process, communication, and decision-making ('who calls legal? who decides to pull the plug?'). A red team engagement is the opposite extreme — a skilled adversarial team actually attacks your live environment over days or weeks, with real techniques, to test whether your defenders detect and respond. A purple team sits in between and collaborative: red and blue work together in real time, the attacker runs a technique and the defender immediately checks 'did we see that?', tuning detections on the spot. Lay out the three for me on a scale of cost and realism, and tell me which one you would run first in an org that has never tested its defences, and why.

You are facilitating a ransomware tabletop, and the quality of the exercise lives entirely in the questions you ask — they should expose decisions the team has never actually rehearsed, not technical trivia. The most valuable ones probe the painful, cross-functional choices: do we pay the ransom — who has the authority to decide, and is it even legal for us? How do we operate the business while systems are down — do we even have offline runbooks? Are our backups actually isolated and tested, or did the ransomware encrypt those too? Who communicates — to staff, customers, regulators, press — and within what legal deadline? When and how do we involve law enforcement, insurance, and outside counsel? Notice none of these are 'how does the encryption work' — they are decisions made under pressure. Give me your five most important discussion questions and explain what gap each one is designed to surface.

Atomic Red Team is a free library of small, precise tests — 'atomics' — each one mapped to a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique, that safely executes the real behaviour of that technique so you can check whether your detections catch it. Instead of waiting to get breached to discover your blind spots, you run the atomic for, say, 'create a scheduled task for persistence' (T1053.005) and then go look in your SIEM: did an alert fire? did the right log even get collected? If nothing lit up, you have found a detection gap on your terms, with a known input, before a real attacker finds it for you. That feedback loop — known technique in, check detection out — is the whole value. Walk me through running one atomic test against your home SOC and how you would judge whether your detection passed or failed.

The objective is what truly separates a red team from a pentester, even though both 'attack' you. A pentester's goal is coverage — find as many exploitable vulnerabilities as possible within scope and time, then report them all so you can fix them; breadth is the deliverable. A red team's goal is to test detection and response — they pick an objective (exfiltrate the crown-jewel data, reach the domain controller) and try to achieve it like a real adversary would, staying quiet, because the real question they answer is 'will the blue team notice and stop us?'. A pentester wants to be loud and thorough; a red teamer wants to be silent and successful. Explain the difference in their goals, and tell me which engagement you would commission to answer 'is our SOC any good?' versus 'how many holes does this new app have?'.

CALDERA is MITRE's open-source automated adversary-emulation platform — it chains together ATT&CK techniques and runs them autonomously against your environment, effectively giving you a robot red team. Its value to a team without a dedicated red team is exactly that automation: you do not need to hire elite offensive talent to find out whether your detections work — you point CALDERA at your lab, let it execute a realistic attack chain (initial access then discovery then lateral movement then exfiltration), and then audit which steps your blue tooling caught and which slipped through silently. It turns 'we cannot afford continuous red teaming' into 'we run an emulated adversary on a schedule and fix the gaps it finds'. Tell me how you would use CALDERA to find detection gaps in your own SOC, and the one limitation of an automated emulator versus a human red teamer.

weeks.pre_flight:
**Tabletop exercise structure:**
```markdown
# Tabletop Exercise — [Scenario Name]

## Participants
- Incident Commander: [name]
- Security Lead: [name]
- Engineering: [name]
- Legal/Comms: [name]

## Scenario
[3-4 sentence description of the incident]

## Injects (delivered during exercise)
- T+0: Initial detection — [what was detected and how]
- T+30min: New information — [additional detail that changes the picture]
- T+60min: Escalation — [complication that increases severity]

## Discussion Questions
1. Who is the incident commander?
2. What is our immediate containment action?
3. Do we need to notify affected users? When?
4. What is our external communication strategy?
5. How do we preserve forensic evidence?
```

**Atomic Red Team — ATT&CK technique simulation:**
```bash
# Install Invoke-AtomicRedTeam (PowerShell)
Install-Module -Name invoke-atomicredteam
Import-Module invoke-atomicredteam
# Run a specific atomic test (T1059.001 = PowerShell)
Invoke-AtomicTest T1059.001
```

**MITRE CALDERA (free, open-source adversary simulation):**
```bash
git clone https://github.com/mitre/caldera.git --recursive
pip3 install -r requirements.txt
python3 server.py --insecure
# Access at http://localhost:8888
```
common_mistakes: Running tabletops without a facilitator — someone must drive the scenario, inject new information, and keep the discussion on track.
Not including legal/comms in tabletops — breach notification, regulatory reporting, and PR are decisions that need the right people in the room.
Treating red team findings as a task list — a red team finding means your detection failed. Fix the detection gap, not just the vulnerability.
Using Atomic Red Team without first baselining your detections — run an atomic test, see if your SIEM alerts, iterate. Without the detection gap analysis, you are just making noise.
Not running post-exercise action items — a tabletop that produces no follow-up tasks was a social exercise, not a security exercise.
weeks.debug_help:
**Invoke-AtomicRedTeam install fails?**
```powershell
# Set execution policy for current user
Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Scope CurrentUser
# Install from PSGallery
Install-Module -Name invoke-atomicredteam -Scope CurrentUser -Force
```

**CALDERA agent not connecting?**
```bash
# Check server is running
curl http://localhost:8888/api/v2/agents
# Deploy a sandcat agent (built-in agent)
# Go to CALDERA UI → Agents → Deploy Agent → select your OS
```

- Timebox each inject to 15-20 minutes of discussion

weeks.title: Building a Career in Security — Specialisation + Portfolio
weeks.context:
Security is a broad field and no one masters all of it. The people who get hired and promoted are specialists with a visible track record. This week you decide your specialisation, build your public portfolio, and learn how to navigate the security job market.

The main specialisation tracks: offensive security (pentesting, red team, bug bounty), defensive security (SOC analyst, detection engineer, incident response), cloud security, AppSec, GRC (governance, risk, compliance), and malware/threat intelligence. Each has different certifications, job titles, and career paths.

Your portfolio is your proof of work. A GitHub with CTF writeups, a blog with vulnerability research, and a list of CVEs or bug bounty findings is more valuable than any certification. Certifications validate that you have studied; portfolio proves you can do.

**Portfolio elements:**
1. GitHub: CTF writeups, tool scripts, detection rules
2. Blog: vulnerability research, technique explanations, lab walkthroughs

common_mistakes: Getting certifications before building practical skills — certs are signals, not skills. Build the skills first, then certify to signal them.
Doing CTFs without writing up your solutions — nobody can see that you solved it. Write it up, publish it, share it. This is your portfolio.
Applying for senior roles before doing bug bounty or CTFs — companies hiring for security roles want to see proof of work. A junior with 10 public writeups beats a senior with a clean LinkedIn.
Not networking in the security community — Twitter/X, Discord (TryHackMe, HackTheBox, NahamSec), DEF CON, BSides conferences. The industry is small and interconnected.
Underselling yourself because security feels like a 'special' field — you have spent 23 weeks building real skills. Own them. Apply.

**Not sure which specialisation to choose?**
Answer these:
1. Do you prefer building/defending or breaking things?
2. Do you prefer code (AppSec, detection engineering) or operations (SOC, IR)?

**Blog platform:**
- Ghost (free tier): professional, security community uses it
- GitHub Pages + Hugo/Jekyll: free, shows technical ability
- Medium: largest audience but no custom domain on free tier

- HackerOne: filter by "Beginner Friendly"
- Bugcrowd: similar filtering
- Start with a program that has a large scope — more surface area = more bugs

weeks.title: Capstone — Earn It
weeks.context:
You have spent 24 weeks learning how to think like an attacker, communicate like a professional, defend like an engineer, and build a career in security. The capstone is not a test — it is a proof of work that demonstrates all of this in a form that is visible to employers and the community.

You will complete three deliverables: a full vulnerability report from a real bug bounty programme or a self-hosted lab environment, a public write-up (blog post) of a technique or finding, and a security portfolio document that ties together everything you have built.

No shortcuts. No AI-generated findings. Every vulnerability you report must be one you found yourself, understood fully, and can explain in detail. The capstone is the start of your career, not the end of a course.

**Prompts that work:**

weeks.pre_flight:
**Capstone deliverables checklist:**

1. Vulnerability Report (real finding or lab-based):
   - At least one finding documented to professional standard
   - Executive summary + technical finding + remediation
   - CVSS score with full vector string
   - Evidence (screenshots, HTTP requests)
   - Submitted to bug bounty OR documented against Juice Shop/HackTheBox

2. Public Write-up (blog post):
   - Minimum 800 words
   - Explains a technique, tool, or vulnerability in your own words
   - Published on your blog (GitHub Pages, Ghost, Medium)
   - Shared on LinkedIn and Twitter/X

3. Portfolio document:
   ```markdown
   # [Your Name] — Security Portfolio

   ## Skills
   - Penetration Testing: [list tools and techniques]
   - Defensive Security: [SIEM, detection, IR]
   - Cloud Security: [AWS tools, compliance frameworks]

   ## Projects
   - [Project 1]: [description, link]
   - [CTF writeups]: [link to blog/GitHub]
   - [Bug bounty submissions]: [public if available]

   ## Certifications / Training
   - [Cert/course + date]

   ## Vulnerability Research
   - [Finding 1]: [severity, type, where]
   ```
common_mistakes: Writing a capstone that only demonstrates tools you can run, not concepts you understand — employers test understanding in interviews, not tool usage.
Publishing a blog post that copies technique documentation — your write-up must add something: your analysis, your mistakes, your observations. Copy-paste is visible and worthless.

Not including your thought process in findings — 'I ran Burp and found XSS' is not a finding. 'I noticed the search parameter was reflected in the response without encoding, so I tested with a basic script tag payload and confirmed execution' is a finding.
Treating the capstone as a final assignment instead of a beginning — this document is the first version of your public profile. Update it every time you find something new.
Waiting until everything is perfect to publish — publish now, improve later. A slightly rough write-up published is infinitely more valuable than a perfect one on your hard drive.
weeks.debug_help:
**Blog post feels too short or thin?**
Add these sections:
- What I tried that didn't work (shows methodology)
- What the root cause is (shows understanding)
- How to test for this in 5 minutes (shows practicality)
- What a developer should do to fix it (shows full-cycle thinking)

**Vulnerability report feels incomplete?**
Check against this template:
- Title: Clear and specific
- Severity + CVSS: with full vector string
- Description: What the vulnerability is
- Reproduction: Step-by-step that a stranger can follow
- Impact: What an attacker gains
- Evidence: Raw HTTP request + response or screenshot
- Remediation: Specific, code-level, actionable

**Portfolio not getting traction?**
- Share in TryHackMe Discord, HackTheBox Discord, r/netsec
- Tag the tool author when you write about their tool
- Engage with comments — a portfolio is the start of a conversation
stretch: Submit your vulnerability report to a real bug bounty programme. Even an Informational finding is a start — document and submit it.
Get your blog post indexed: submit it to Hacker News, Reddit r/netsec, and LinkedIn. Track the views.
Apply for 3 security roles this week — analyst, junior pentester, or security engineer. The capstone is your portfolio; use it.
Book OSCP, eJPT, or PNPT for 3 months from now — give yourself a deadline for your first certification.
